speechtext:
Practically all the remarks that have been made on this subject have been in the nature of a general discussion on the principles of immigration. Evidence has been adduced to show that the state of the present immigrants in this country is not what it should be; and while some may endeavour to interpret our efforts to show to the minister and to the government what those conditions are, particularly as regards the West, as being designed or intended to be obstructive, my firm conviction is that on the part of any hon gentleman with whom I am acquainted or have conversed, there is no intention to obstruct. It is certainly my belief that the evidence I propose to adduce
S upply-Im rniyra tion

as well as that of my colleagues is evidence that should be placed before the country. I have endeavoured time and again to point out the conditions that obtain, and we believe these conditions are not generally known throughout Canada. Consequently, we believe it is in the interest of Canada and the Canadian people as a whole that these things should be placed upon Hansard.
As I was stating, when I was on my feet before, to me fell the task of adjourning the debate on the night of March 20. It is rather difficult to co-ordinate my remarks of that night with the few remarks which I shall make to-day; but it seemed to me that we were then jockeyed into a position where, at a late hour of the night, it was left for three successive members of the Progressive group to carry on the debate. That is the reason why I rose and was making extensive remarks when it was suggested that the debate be adjourned and that I continue my remarks to-day.
At that time, I had stated that it was my belief that the evidence that had been placed upon Hansard during the last few days of the debate in regard to this question, would make really good evidence if it were handed to our prospective immigrants. I was not advocating that this should be done; but if, by chance, it was taken to those countries from which we hope to draw immigrants, it *would at least be very enlightening for them to read those speeches, particularly if in one hand they had the pamphlets that were printed by the Western Canada Colonization Company, or those beautiful lithographed booklets which the Immigration department from time to time send into foreign countries to persuade people to come to Canada and settle.
Speaking more or less in a local sense-and I notice that is the habit of the majority of hon. members who have so far spoken on this question-I wish to place a little more evidence on Hansard to-day. One of the latest letters I have received comes from a hardheaded Scotchman in western Canada, a man whom I have known for twenty years, a good conservative Scotchman. In his letter he complains that he had sold a carload of oats which he had sent to Fort William, and he had likewise sold some oats on the street. He received sixteen cents per bushel less for the oats which he sold on the street than he received for the carload he shipped. His shipping point is only 730 miles west of Fort William, and he wmnders why with a freight rate approximately of ten cents per hundred pounds, sixteen cents per bushel should be 
subtracted from the amount he received on the carload sent to Fort William. I point this out only to show that what I have complained of many times, namely, that some of these institutions in the West seem to be almost laws unto themselves.
Of course, remedies have been suggested from time to time for these evils that we complain of. I do not wish to condemn, nor to have this interpreted as a desire on my part to condemn, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), for I have great faith in him; but we are told at the present time to produce a better quality of pork, beef, butter, cheese and all other farm products, so that we may be able to compete with Denmark, Belgium, and all other countries that export these commodities. For the past forty years in western Canada we have been producing the best quality of grain known in the world, namely, No. 1 hard wheat, and when we had produced a commodity of one hundred per cent value, what happened with our wheat? Why, immediately vested interests in this country came to former governments and obtained the right to rob us by mixing this grain. That condition obtains to-day, and that is what we get when we produce a hundred per cent article. That is one thing that is the matter with agriculture in the West at the present time, and one reason, by the way, why I have always pleaded that the producer should have an opportunity of presenting his case before commissions appointed from time to time, so that their grievances may be remedied.
These are only small items, but they affect each and every individual in the West who is engaged in raising grain. I cited this case to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) last year. I regret sincerely that the minister is not in his seat at this time; but I cite the case of a neighbour of mine who sent a carload of wheat to Fort William asking that it be stored. The wheat was presumably stored, and anyone who stores wheat knows that it is cleaned wheat that is stored. This man received a bill amounting to $2.29 for storage, and he uras paid 33 cents for 26 bushels of screenings, cracked wheat, that were taken out of his grain. That is the condition I pointed out to the minister from my place in this House, and his reply was that he would look into the matter. The man who owned the grain has never heard anything about the matter since, nor have I, and that is only another illustration of conditions that obtain in our western country. I would tell prospective immigrants that there are hundreds of schools in western Canada closed because of the inability of people to

Supply-Immigration
pay taxes. That is a well-known fact, and it. is a truth that applies to very large areas not alone in Alberta and Saskatchewan but elsewhere as well. I would also tell them that in nearly all judicial districts in western Canada in sheriffs' safes there are from 1,000 to 4,000 judgments. That too is a well established fact. If we told the prospective immigrant that such a state of things existed, he would ask; What is the matter with agriculture in Canada that such conditions can prevail? There is something else also which hon. members may regard as of little moment, but which I can assure the committee is, on the contrary, of much importance. (3ur Dominion government in the past have sold school lands, entering into contract with the purchaser and selling those lands at a capitalization of five per eent. This has happened, for instance, in the district from which I come where a goodly number of people bought lands under these terms. We all know very well that there were visitations of Providence in the way of drought, hail, rust, grasshoppers and all the other evils which have afflicted the people and which have gone to affect the proceeds of their crops. What do we see? Those people wTho were unable, through these Providential circumstances, to meet their obligations found themselves compelled by the Dominion government to meet an additional two per cent on their obligation, their indebtedness being thus capitalized at seven per cent, as though the visitation of Providence were not a sufficient burden. It does seem to me that the government were not in any way obliged to add that two per cent, and considering the circumstances of the case I think they might well remit this seven per cent which was inflicted upon the people at that time in connection with these lands.
In short, if we are going to send out any propaganda, I would advise that we tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and then see how many people we could get by so doing. I have here the figures in connection with immigration to and emigration from the United States alone. I might inform the committee that the figures in regard to this country I have obtained from the Canadian Year Book for the year 1922, while for the other figures I am indebted to the records of the United States Department of Labour. The first figures I have are for the year 1911, and it would be well for us to remember that they relate to a country where conditions are supposed to he very much the same as they are in. Canada. And while we thought that we were drawing immigration from the United States it turns out that in
the final result there has been a distinct, a decided, loss to 1he people of Canada as compared w'ith the country to rhe south of us. In 1911, we had a gain of 52,000: in 1912, a gain of 68,000; in 1913 a gain of 55,000; in 1914 a gain of 12,000. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in 1915 we had one of the largest crops in Canadian history, particularly in the West. I mention this fact only to show that because there happens to be a big crop in the West it does not necessarily follow' that the population will be beneficially affected. In the four instances I have cited it will be seen that we had gains. But in 1915, when this big crop occurred, what happened? We had a loss of 30,000 people; in 1 other words, 30,000 people left Canada more than came into the country from the United States. In 1916, another year that was not bad, we had a total loss of 68.000 of people going to the United States. In 1917, there was a total loss of 48,000 from Canada; but in 1918 the tables were turned and we had
36,000	of a gain. In 1919, however, we had again a loss of 22,000; in 1920, a loss of 47,000; in 1921, a loss of 30,000; and in 1922 a loss of 17,000. To sum up, we lost by actual emigration to the United States alone, in the decade I have mentioned, 39,000 people. Now, there is something wrong; and each and every one of these 39,000 people will testify to just what is the matter with colonization conditions in Canada. And whether it be a matter for rectification on the part of the government-and I believe that the government can do very much to make conditions better and more equitable in this country-, the fact remains that 39,000 of our people have gone to the United States, 39,000 missionaries who will tell the truth, perhaps too luridly. And that is the reason or at least one of the reasons, why we may not expect a large influx of immigration from the United States-a country which, by the way, gives us our best settlers-until such time as conditions are, in their estimation at least, as good in Canada as they are in the country to which they are going back. I made the statement that in all civilized countries, at least where the white peoples have come from, agriculture was bleeding to death. And I have authority for the statement. In Australia, they have borrowed moneys for the purpose of settling people on the land, and as nearly as I can ascertain, capitalizing it at only five per cent, which I may say is my own estimate, the amounts borrowed will produce the sum of $250 for every settler going into Australia. In the plan we contemplate we provide approximately $500, or twice the amount which in Australia the gov-
Supply-Immigration

ernment, or whatever patronizing source it comes from, is prepared to give. Now, I do not see why Canada, with all her potential wealth, should be obliged to pay $2 as against SI in comparison with Australia for the immigrants that come into the country.

speechtext:
In the United States there has been before congress a bill asking for $300,000,000 to assist agriculture there. Now, in spite of their high tariff wall, the purpose of which we are told is to protect American agriculture, it seems that they still realize that agricidture is not receiving sufficient encouragement and it is now being given patronage from the government. Three hundred million dollars is a huge sum, and I am not advocating such financial assistance to agriculture. All I contend for is that we may have equal opportunities to take the potential wealth from the soil-opportunities which I believe have been largely denied us, or at least if we have not been actually denied them we have been prevented from retaining what we consider our fair share of that wealth when produced.
In the western country we have vast areas which are still unsettled, and I think that any settlement scheme should be carried out under the supervision of the government and not through the Western Canada Colonization Association. The Minister (Mr. Stewart) is well aware of the conditions in the West, and he knows the importance of community life to those who settle there. I have often considered a community plan which would concentrate the people and give them the opportunity of having their schools and other public institutions close in. One of the great drawbacks even in the organized districts in western
tMr. Gould.]
Canada to-day is the lack of school facilities and the difficulty experienced in securing the attendance of children from remote farms. Consolidation has been tried in a few places, but I would like to see it attempted in a broader form whereby townships or divisions of townships might be brought together and roads and other conveniences provided so that the people would receive more of the benefits of community life, the absence of which is one of the great drawbacks to settlement in western Canada. Imagine a man taking his wife and family into a remote district two or three, and very often five or six, miles from his nearest neighbour. Naturally enough the woman's heart is broken. I recommend this important feature to the attention of the minister and I hope' something will be done along these lines to make prairie life more attractive.
I have under my hand an advertisement sent out by the Bank of Montreal in which it is stated:
Canada in the past tfiree years has exported surplus vegetable and animal products to the value of $1,900,000,000.
That naturally would strike the mind of the immigrant as a huge sum, indeed it would impress anyone at first sight, but when divided up among our agriculturists the sum per capita is comparatively insignificant. Taking the farming population of Canada as approximately fifty per cent of the total, and multiplying it by three, the number of years covered, we have as a result 13,500,000 farmers, each of whom would receive out of this huge total of $1,900,000,000, the small sum of $140.75, or taking it on the basis of a family of five, the sum of $703.75. Neither sum is such as to cause the average farmer or his family to go into ecstacies. And yet this represents merely his gross return. I submit that transportation costs and taxation must be deducted say, $100 per capita, or $500 per family. Deduct this from the figures I have already given and we find how little the agriculturist has left to provide clothes, fuel and the other necessaries of life. It is at once apparent that the farmer is faced with an absolute physical impossibility in attempting to make a living under such conditions; and yet these are the conditions that obtain.

Mr. Chairman, the question of immigration has since confederation been an important and pressing problem. We have through the years framed various policies with a view of increasing the numbers of our people, and whether our efforts have achieved a measure consistent with the amount of public money expended is perhaps open to some question.
In announcing his proposals the minister indicated that he was not bringing before the House any, as he described it, brand new policy; he informed us that he was taking the middle course. His position could perhaps have been more adequately described had he suggested that he was sitting on the fence, and I am sure he has earned the at-

Supply-Immigration
tacks which are usually made upon those who assume that attitude, because, if I mistake not, his emotions must have run through the whole gamut of human sentiments when one considers the reluctant expessions of appreciation which came to him from some members of his own party and, in addition, the sledge hammer blows which have been directed at his policy by other members supporting the government. I think, perhaps, the minister must have had in his mind the injunction which many years ago was given to one of the leaders of the Jewish people when he was enjoined not to make "any graven image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth." It seems to me, that the position of the minister can only be compared to that of the heroine who was "There twixt heaven and earth suspended while the bell tolled to. and fro."
I think it is desirable, Mr. Chairman, that we should pay some attention to the census statistics in so far as they may be of value in determining the policy of parliament in connection with this problem. The House, I think is indebted to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) in indicating the exact history of our emigration problem. I would like to suggest that the statistics of Canadian emigration, so far as they are disclosed to us by the United States, show that in the decade between 1901 and 1910 some 179,226 people left this country; whereas in the following decade, between 1911 and 1920 some 742,000 odd emigrated from Canada. We find also, if we take the decade-and I do not intend to weary the House unduly with figures- from 1911 to 1921 that, allowing for the natural increase, according to the figures there must be a loss to this country of something like, 1,200,000 people. Now let me quote one or two other figures with regard to immigration during the past two years. In the fiscal year ending March, 1922, approximately 90,000 people came to Canada; the year previous the arrivals numbered 148,000 odd; and in the year 1920 some 117,000 odd. So that last year, if we except the war years from 1916 to 1919 the low water mark in inmmigration was reached taking our history as far back as 1902.
In connection with these facts I want to make a few observations. It seems to me that we have two problems to solve-the problem of emigration and the problem of immigration. I have already indicated the extent of the emigration to the United States as indicated by the figures I have given. I
would like to point out that that emigration is a voluntary emigration; it is not induced by any advertisements on the part of the United States government. That is a distressing feature of 'the situation because experience shows that that sort of emigration, that is voluntary emigration, is made up of the young, the industrious and the ambitious. That is an unfortunate fact. What is the reason that the best of our manhood and womanhood are leaving the country? Occasionally in former days people in emigrating were influenced by religious considerations; at other times they were influenced by political considera-' tions. To-day there can be no question at all but that the reason for the emigration to the United States is due to the fact that our economic conditions are not all they should be. It is quite apparent that the emigration to the United States is due to the desire either to escape the existing economic conditions, or else to obtain better economic conditions. I mention these facts not because I am discouraged; on the contrary I am not; I mention them because they constitute an appalling and a tragic fact that our own people- our own Canadian and Canadianized people -are unable to obtain that measure of satisfaction which they look for in this country and are therefore seeking a refuge in a foreign land. That is not an easy thing for a Canadian to do, it is not an easy thing for a Canadianized individual to do, because it necessarily means the severance of the ties of kinship, the severance of the ties of devotion which binds everyone to this land. Therefore, I say, Mr. Chairman, that the primary duty of this government is to investigate this condition with regard to emigration.	"
In this connection I am reminded of the statement of Sir Andrew Macphail. Speaking some time ago at McGill university he said; referring to the government:
You put a little less stress on this policy of immigration until you are quite sure you can keep the immigrants you pay for.
After some further references to the number of people leaving the country he said:
The people of Canada cannot save themselves by this process of immigration any more than could the Romans by their system of slavery.

immigration from this country. It seems to me that the government should take this matter of emigration into consideration,' not in any panicky mood because there is no necessity for panic. I think they should ascertain, as far as it can be humanly ascertained, the existing cause and then fearlessly apply the remedy whatever it may be. I am not going into the causes for emigration; it is not necessary to do so at this particular time. I do suggest, however, that if you want to keep people in this country there must be a determined effort to reduce the cost of living, there must be a determined effort to reduce the burden of taxation under which this country is reeling at the present time. Now what is the government's attitude toward this question of emigration? What is their policy in regard to this important matter? I suppose that if I were to ask the Minister of Finance he would tell me in Asquithian language "Wait and see." It appears to me that the government are assuming the fatalistic position that little can be done to stem the tide of emigration. I do not agree with that view at all. Personally I would vote for a very definite, a very clear cut, and a very courageous programme for the purpose of stopping the emigration from our land.
There is another interesting fact to which I would draw the attention of the House in connection with the census figures. At the census of 1901 the figures indicated that 62.3 per cent of our population was rural. The census of 1911 indicated that 54 per cent was rural, a decrease of some 8 per cent in that decade. The census figures of 1921 indicate that 50.3 per cent was rural, a further decrease of something like 4 per cent. There must b some reason for the rural depopulation that is evidently going on. I mention that because I am impressed with this fact: That every person who migrates from the land into an urban centre becomes a potential emigrant from the country. The person who leaves the land and endeavours to compete in the city necessarily finds difficulty in carrying on there owing to the specialized conditions prevailing, and therefore I think it is important, if we can check the rural depopulation, that we should do so. At least we should make some determined effort to ascertain and remedy the cause, and thus to my mind shut off one of the potential taps leading to emigration from Canada.
May I be permitted to mention what occurs to me as one or two important reasons for rural depopulation? There is, of course, the lure of the city so-called, but more important than that are the hardships incident

to a pioneering land, the difficulties and hardships which must be overcome. I for one regret that during our entire history we have never seen fit, or at least on very few occasions, to pay any honour to those who pioneered in Canada. We have multitudes of honours, titles and otherwise, for those who have achieved political success, and we have the same conditions prevailing for those who have achieved some measure of commercial success, but for the man who lives on the frontier we have never been able to award or accord to him what seems to me his fitting recognition. *
The second cause for rural depopulation is necessarily the high production costs, and I use the word " high " as compared with the amount received by the producer in return for his efforts. It seems to me that these causes can be ascertained with a fair degree of accuracy. What are the causes which create high production costs in relation to the returns received. First of all I want to suggest, and I know my friends to the right will entirely disagree with me, that chief among these deterrents, chief among the difficulties is the tariff. We have built for forty years on a policy designed to put tall chimneys in eastern Canada. It seems to me that our policy for a time at least should have that degree of orientation which will enable farmers to reap the just reward for their efforts. Some hon. gentlemen may think that the farmers do receive a just reward for their efforts. But I presume that no one will dispute the view taken by the president of the Dominion Bank in his annual statement for the year 1922. He says:
Of the unfavourable features, immigration returns are most disappointing and, so far, it appears that no sound measures have been devised by governments, or others, that will bring any improvement. The many attractive features that Canada has to offer to settlers have been more than offset by the poor results that farming operations have shown in the past two or three years.
He goes on:
Excessive taxation is a great detriment, and there can be no relief while provincial governments and municipalities so freely spend money which they obtain from the public with astonishing ease.
Why he eliminated the Dominion government from his observations I do not know.

Another important element, and I propose to give the government credit for having made some progress, lies in the fact that our whole country, our whole transportation system at least, seems to be in the hands of combines, combinations which have as their avowed purpose apparently the raising of rates to the extent that the traffic will bear. I am sure that hon. members of this House cannot but be impressed with the evidence that has been given before the Lake Shipping, Commission and the evidence also taken before the special committee on Agriculture, from which it appears that not only the railways and the ocean companies, but also our own National Railways and our own Canadian Government Merchant Marine have been to some extent at least implicated in this effort to maintain rates at what they deemed to be a proper standard instead of, as the people have a right to expect, competing with other railways and other transportation systems. The government, I think, is entitled to some credit for having undertaken these investigations. I think, too, they are entitled to credit for having inaugurated or at least given promise of inaugurating a policy which will do much to eradicate combines when and where they are found.
Another important element, it seems to me, that must be considered before an immigration policy can secure that measure of success which is desirable is to free western lands from the group of exploiters and speculators who now have them under control. I think that perhaps in consultation with provincial governments a progressive and scientific system of taxation could be undertaken with regard to the speculatively held lands in order that they will either be put to productive use or come back into the hands of the state, and thereby be of service to intending immigrants.
These, Mr. Chairman, are only a few of the difficulties which confront the farmer in western Canada, and I believe, for that matter, in all parts of Canada to-day. I think some effort should be made in order to relieve him of these burdens which, to my mind, unnecessarily make his position perilous.

I think the government should direct its best energy, and give primary consideration to that particular problem.
With regard to the question of immigration itself, I have no objection to a vigorous immigration policy. I have not the slightest objection to bringing people into this country who can, if conditions are favourable, make themselves into efficient citizens. I have no objection to a well-considered immigration policy, provided that that immigration policy is synchronised with an efficient, if I might so call it, emigration policy, or a policy designed to prevent emigration. I do not ask that all immigration must be stopped until the emigration problem is solved. I think these two problems should go side by side. If this House will give to the problem of emigration its serious and undivided attention, and at the same time co-ordinate that with a policy of immigration, progress will be made.
As regards the problems which touch the farmers of western Canada, the problems to which I refer, and which are the exciting cause of the emigration which exists to-day,
I do not ask the government simply to look in the direction of a solution of those problems; I do not suggest to them that there should be what the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) called a mere "molecular movement" in the direction of reform. They should courageously undertake the solution of those problems in order to accomplish some results in preventing further emigration from our country. After all-and I have said this before in this House-the best immigration advertisement is a contented and prosperous farmer. I ask the Acting Minis-
ter of Immigration how he can expect farrm ers or others brought in from foreign lands, unacclimatised to our conditions, unfamiliar with our life, to succeed where we have today men who have had the advantage of free land and who, despite their strenuous efforts, have not achieved that measure of success which, at least, would constitute them the best of immigration agents for this country.
There is, however, one point in regard to which I have very serious objection to the government's policy. I refer to the Canada Colonization Association. This scheme was bom in the heads of various transportation and manufacturing interests. The Canada Colonization Association is the subsidiary and the inheritor of the Western Canada Colonization Company. It is now, as the minister has indicated to us, a headless organization. The government has apparently no written agreement with that organization; but it has agreed to pay them SI00,000 this year, of which $40,000 has already been paid. I have looked with some interest at the advertisements of this association, and I find amongst other things that they tell us that the whole wide world is their field of activity for immigration purposes. They tell us that, as regards the United States, there will be hundreds of agents canvassing on behalf of this country, drumming up immigration, I think they call it, before the snow flies. In reply I may say that the question of assistance to immigrants coming to Canada has been given careful consideration, but it was felt that, in view of our present financial condition, the department would not be warranted in asking for an appropriation for this purpose at the present time. However, I may point out that the Canada Colonization Association, with headquarters in Winnipeg, Manitoba, has rather elaborate plans for assisting immigration, and I wish to suggest that you get in touch with Mr. M. A. Brown, the vice-president of this association, at the Bank of Hamilton building, Winnipeg.
For your information I am enclosing herewith copy of the Immigration Act and regulations, which will give you full information of the qualifications required of immigrants coming to Canada at the present time.
So that it is perfectly clear that on the 14th October last the minister had made no restrictions, and, in fact, the Canada Colonization Association had made no restrictions, with regard to the field of their activities. But the situation seems to have been changed, because we find now, according to the words of the minister, that this association is restricted to the United States, the most fertile field, the best field for immigration for this country, and it has no authority or apparently exercises no authority beyond the confines of the North American continent. We also find that although this company had advertised that hundreds of agents would be carrying on, drumming up the work of immigration in the United States before the snow commenced to fly, according to the minister only some sixty agents are operating to-day. Now why this state of coma that characterizes this organization at the present time? I suggest that in this vital and important matter the government has no right to abdicate its function to the Canada Colonization Association, a headless organization of this character, which has in no measure lived up to the promises it made, which has no written agreement with the government, or perhaps if anything only a verbal contract, and whose responsibility is based on such verbal contract. Therefore I most strenuously object to the 89 J
government carrying on any further negotiations with that association. I am quite satisfied that that position represents the feeling of a large number of members of this House. The promoters and associates of this organization have themselves withdrawn support from it. Then why should the parliament of Canada now bolster it up further with an appropriation of $60,000? I think that the government can without any loss of dignity simply refuse to subsidize the organization further and put this matter of possible immigration from the United States into the hands of its own responsible agents. In addition to that, those members of the House who have written letters expressing, to some degree at least, confidence in the organization have repudiated the suggestion that they meant to convey that the government should give any financial assistance to the organization. I say, therefore, that the government can and should have no further dealings with the association; In any event I am perfectly satisfied that after the publicity this association has now received its work will be of little avail in the future. '
Let me say in conclusion that, if I judge rightly, the country does demand a vigorous policy designed to prevent indiscriminate immigration but which will bring into the country those who can make a success under the conditions that prevail to-day. Personally, I have the greatest faith in this country. I see no reason why we should at this time be discouraged or why we should lose faith. I think there is great hope for the future; and I believe that if we bend our energies to the consideration of these problems we can accomplish something of real service to Canada. We are fortunately situated. We are not embroiled in the many difficulties and entanglements which are so typical of European and other countries to-day. We have a great opportunity in this country, and we simply need to apply ourselves to the task. I am confident, as a Canadian, having in mind the lofty type of patriotism, characterizing our citizenship and believing that our people have courage and devotion to their country, that we can achieve success even though some hon. gentlemen seem to think that that is out of the question nowadays.

And speaking of our farmers' achievements, we know what they have been able to do in competition with outsiders at any of the great expositions that have taken place, especially on the American continent. I speak from memory, but I think I am safe An saying that at the great international fat stock show at Chicago last year Canada carried off 19 out of the 25 prizes. So that the trouble rests not with our farmers or with the country itself; there must be something wrong with the policy which we have had since confederation. We have ' heard a great deal, and I know that much has been said from this corner, in regard to the conditions in this country; and hon. members have stood up in this House and told US'practically that we did' not kpqw what we were talking about. Those hon. members have offered us sympathy. Well, Sir, I want to tell hon. gentlemen that the fttrmers of western Canada are not comipg here looking for , any sympathy ; they are asking for a square deal, for a chance to make good, for an equal opportunity with others: My hon. friend (Mr. Marler) the other night in an excellent speech told us that what we wanted was courage. I would ask hoh. gentlemen of this House to consider for a moment the character of the men and women who have carried civilization into those western plains, who have endured the hardships and the toils of a pioneer life, who have combatted through hail, frost and insect pests' and other natural afflictions, and; then say whether these people are lacking in courage.
We are told that one of the solutions to remedy our adverse conditions is to reduce our standard of living and do as our forefathers did in the old pioneering days. It is even suggested that the peasant type of settler should he brought in from Europe. Mr. Chairman,'since when have the British Aock become mih weaklings. Are we going to admit that the ebinbination of the "two greatest races that the world has ever known is about to fall down in the development of this country and is to be supplanted by the peasant type of iMmigrant from Europe? I think it is time that we as'Canadians woke up and faced this matter squarely. " ' '
We hear a great deal about the necessity of the farniers reditcihg their standard of living and undergoing the privations of pioneer dayS: - Perhaps we Have all gone a little too far' in the high standard of living.. But "why should we expect' the' farmers to be the only

class to reduce their standard? Would it be unfair to say to our manufacturers, for instance, that perhaps they could do something along this line as well and so be able to produce goods at a price which we could afford to pay?
The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) last week in a very eloquent address told, us about an ingenious young Irish immigrant who by following out a course of semistarvation rose to a veiy high position in our public life. Well, while he was talking I wondered to what heights that immigrant might have risen had he remained at home and applied the same ingenuity and ability. He might not only have become member of parliament, but he plight even be the ruling power in the Emerald Isle to-day. I think some hon. gentlemen, were led to believe that such a successful career as depicted by the hon .member for Springfield was only possible in Canada. Let.ipe remind the committee that in Great Britain , notwithstanding her great burden of debt and other troubles, there are still possibilities for the individual who possesses ability and . application. In this connection we cannot forget the wonderful career of that little boy in a Welsh village who rose by sheer ability until to-day he is regarded as one of the greatest, statesman the world has ever known. It is not the material resources of a country that make for great statesmen. Recently I read an article by; Mr. Otto H. Kahn concerning British-American relations, in the course of which he said:
It is not the possession of raw materials and other latent resources, it is not the bounty of nature, it is the qualities and efforts of its people that make a nation great.
The immigration estimates now before us show a large increase for the purpose of bringing in new settlers. The question naturally arises, what have we got to offer our settlers today. Comparing present conditions with those of twenty years ago, our settlers were then able to take up free land. If a man took up a quarter section and was not able to make his farming operations pay his overhead was not piling up. At that time we had a very energetic railway policy, and the workmen engaged on railway construction provided ready purchasers for anything the settler produced and if in the fall season he needed some ready cash he could go out with his team and work on the railway grade and thus secure enough ready money to carry him over the winter. We hear a great deal to-day about the men who put up with hardships in those days, and that they were not even able to secure postage stamps. That may be true, but while they were waiting for postage
stamps their overhead expenses were not accumulating to any alarming extent. Now immigrants are to be placed on land of an average value of $18 to $20 an acre, and unless he has the requisite amount of capital to purchase his farm outright he must be successful from the very beginning, otherwise interest charges, taxes and the high cost of living .are going to force him out of business.
I am not going to relate in detail the conditions now prevailing in the. West; those have been already presented at sufficient length. But I would just like to say that conditions are undoubtedly bad, and our people are getting so discouraged that unless this government can give us some policy which will instil fresh hope into our people, I fear for the results. I do not suggest that we should not allow anyone to enter Canada until we get conditions perfect, btit I do say that if the government could give us Some ray of hope for these people so that we can tell them: The government is honestly endeavouring by bringing in a new 'policy-because it has been amply' demonstrated that our present policy is not producing the results expected-a policy that we hope will improve your condition, such a message would mean a great deal to these people and they would take fresh courage, because I believe there is: not a single farmer who would not dig in and work harder to pull through if we could give him some ray of hope that he would succeed.
After the arguments that have been advanced in this, House the government and the minister (Mr. Stewart) should be fully seized of the fact that we are not in favour of the colonization scheme which he has placed before the committee. I hope the government will fully realize the responsibility they will be assuming in letting it appear to the country that this Canada Colonization Association scheme is being backed by the Dominion government. It may be safely assumed that the high-powered salesmen who will be engaged to drum , up settlers, having in view only their commission of $320 if they land a settler ' on a half-section, will pajmt.sptne very,rosy pictures to prospective immigrants, and when these immigrants find, conditions have been misrepresented naturally they wifi look to the government to assume responsibility for the statements which they were led to believe were true.
I do not believe in criticizing any sehejnp without endeavouring to offer some suggestions along constructive lines, I believe that the first essential in keeping settlers on the land is to have the right kind of land settlement policy. The next is the reconstruction

of rural life around various forms of co-operative enterprise. The old policy of bringing settlers into the country and leaving them to shift for themselves will not do. They must be taught the best methods to ensure success. And, furthermore, hand in hand with, or rather in advance of an aggressive policy to obtain this type of settler, there must be action by the federal government to ensure that those already on the land and those about to come may have adequate markets and marketing facilities, to the end that they may obtain some reasonable profit for their labour and investment.
I have made a note here of four suggestions that I think might well receive the serious consideration of the government. In the first place, there is the question of a reduction of the tariff. The people are getting discouraged because they have always felt that the Liberal government stood for a low tariff. The very fact that the people turned out the old government indicated their dissatisfaction with the then prevailing conditions, and they are looking for a change.
Another suggestion would be a reduction in our transportation costs and equalization of our freight rates so that we may be able to get our goods out more cheaply. I would submit also the desirability of considering a long term credit scheme for agricultural loans. I do not offer this suggestion with the idea that the farmers should be given more credit; possibly one of the things we have been up against in the past is the fact that we have had too much credit. But a three months' loan to the farmer is of no use. The United States is realizing the necessity of taking some action along this line. If the government could do something to assist in the providing of capital with which we could replace the present loans that are piling up at a high rate of interest, the effect of which in the end will only be to drive us out of the country; if we could have these extended over a long term so that we might have some hope of ultimately getting out of debt, . I am sure it would mean a great deal.
Another suggestion is that there be some encouragement of co-operative enterprises. I do not refer now merely to the little cooperative store; we must get some method of pooling our grain and our live stock. After all, this is not purely a farmers' question; it is a national question, and if the government could offer encouragement along this line the result would be very beneficial indeed. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) expressed the view the other day that his part of the country at least was
FMr. Lucas.]
over-institutionalized. I largely agree with that view, not as respects schools, but as respects almost every other line. Speaking about our grain, any hon. members who have travelled through the West will bear me out when I say that in every little town along the railway-and they come every seven os eight miles-one is impressed with the large number of elevators that have been built I think I am safe in saying that in practically every little town there are from three to five elevators. That means that, in the first place, there is the capital outlay; then there is the local buyer, who is actively engaged only about three months in the year but who receives an annual salary; then there are inspectors going up and down the country, and there are the head offices with their
5 p.m. general managers and staffs of clerks. That load is getting too heavy for the farmers to carry. The same conditions exist in our banking system; in every little town there are two or more banks; there is hardly a town in the West which has only one. Going from here to Toronto via the lake shore route one cannot help being impressed by the fact that three lines of railways paraL each other, requiring three stations and three sets of employees in every little town. That is what our competitive system has done for us, and it is something I think the government should take into its serious consideration.
I hope that the government will bring in some policy that we may be able to take back to our people with the view of giving them a little hope and inspiring them with fresh courage to go on for the future. I believe we have in Canada, not one of the finest countries, but the finest country in the world. It is a matter of regret for me to see hon. members, as has sometimes been the case in this House, seek to obtain party advantage rather than face squarely the issue before the country. The time of the House was taken up noticeably last year in an effort to place the responsibility for our railway situation upon one party or the other; in fact, we fought the election campaign of December 6, 1921, all over again. I do not think that is what we are here for. If we could get away from that sort of thing; if we could forget who is responsible for what has happened in the past and get down to a solution of the problems actually before us, it would be a good thing for the country. The people are demanding that we give them a lead in the matter of bringing them out of the very serious conditions now prevailing. I hope therefore, that hon. members in every quarter

New Ontario offers to-day the greatest field in the world for colonization. The constituency that I have the honour to represent has nearly doubled its population in the last two decades. Throughout that broad section of the northland the farmer is happy and prosperous and new land is continually being taken up by a hardy type of settlers who have gone into that country to remain. Our colonization problem has more to do with the getting of a suitable class of immigrants.

Let me illustrate what occurred in my own constituency. Twenty-five or thirty years ago Father Paradis went to Michigan and induced fifty or sixty families to come into the district which is in the vicinity of Verner. The second generation of these hardy pioneers comprise to-day the most prosperous farmers in Ontario. I invite hon. members, either of the Progressive party or from among those who represent the cities, to look through the train windows as they pass through Nipissing and see what has been accomplished by settlers who were reclaimed from the United States. The same conditions obtain along the three national railways. These hardy settlers followed the lumbering concerns into the wooded lands of the north. They cleared those lands and developed their farms under the most difficult conditions; but, endowed as they were with courage and possessing large families, they have succeeded in transforming that lumbering country into a prosperous and happy farming community.
This process of colonization is still going on, but let it not be thought for one moment that the difficulties which the settler has to face in northern Ontario are any less than those which the settler in the West has to overcome. The farmer who has gone into New Ontario has had many obstacles to surmount, and one of his greatest handicaps has been the forest fires from which the western farmer does not suffer. All through that northern section the farmers have established comfortable homes, with large outbuildings, and the value of their lands is constantly growing. In my own constituency the population in 1901 was 24,931; in 1911, it was 43,679; and in 1921, it ha'd risen to 58,525. This constituency is largely rural, and thirty years ago it was almost a wilderness. At the present time the lands contiguous to the three railways which traverse new Ontario are gradually being taken up by settlers of the same class. There has also been a continuous influx of the same type of farmers across the border into the district, of Abitibi, in the province of Quebec, and to-day that section of Quebec is peopled by from fifteen to eighteen thousand happy and prosperous farmers. Again I say that if we are going to settle our immigration problem in a satisfactory manner, the class of settlers brought to the land is a paramount consideration'; to my mind it forms the crux of the whole situation. The French Canadians in northern Ontario have had to face other difficulties besides those attendant upon the development of the land. The province of Ontario does not give the French Canadian minority the same privileges or the same treatment that the English minority enjoys in the province of Quebec. Nevertheless, those men have clung tenaciously to the lands they have developed, and to-day they still have confidence in the good will of the English speaking majority of Ontario and look forward to an early settlement of this disability which presses upon them so heavily.
There has been no exodus from the farms in northern Ontario. We have there a class of farmers who, during the days of prosperity, laid aside a sufficient amount to carry them through the period of depression. The prosperous farmer in the north listened to the counsels of those more familiar with our economical conditions and to-day are passing through the prevailing hard times without complaint.

In connection with disabilities from which the farmers in that district may suffer there is one matter to which I wish to draw the attention of the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization. At the outlet of lake Timiskaming, during the past winter, lumbering operations have been carried on on a very large scale. At a point on the Ottawa river on the Quebec side, where the stream is quite narrow, six hundred men have taken out
200,000	logs. On the Ontario side, since the 4th of October, one thousand men have taken out 450,000 logs. The results have been that on both sides of the river there are two great areas covered with from four to six feet of slash. On the Quebec side, is located Kippawa Pulp and Paper Company's plant which cost fifteen millions to build and which would be jeopardized were a fire to take place in these immense quantities of slash. I wish to go on record as stating these facts because there is at the present moment a great deal of anxiety among the people of that section of Ontario on account of the conditions I have described.
In conclusion I wish to say that there is one feature about the agricultural conditions in New Ontario which has contributed a great deal to the prosperity of that country; it is the fact that they have a market practically at their own doors. The mining industry has undoubtedly helped very largely towards the successful development of that north country. But even so the government of Ontario have unlimited confidence in the possibilities of the northern district and are now extending the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to within 130 miles of James Bay. It is safe to say that as soon as this railway is in operation we will see a continuous inflow of immigration into that northern country. There never was a more opportune time for the farmer who is prepared to accept the hardships that necessarily accompany the development of northern lands to go in and settle in that country. Mother nature has been generous but she does not easily give up her treasures. Still we invite that class of settlers to go into the north where the prospects of creating a home under the most favourable conditions now exist and advantages of the most promising character may be reaped.

But even if we take into consideration these facts, are the farmers of Manitoba in such a prosperous con. dition as one might infer from the speech to which I refer? I have in my hand a copy of the Manitoba Free Press of February 6, 1922. The Free Press is a western paper, imbued with the western spirit, a paper that is always boosting for the West, a paper that believes to-day in a vigorous and energetic immigration policy. Yet, in that issue some very illuminating figures are quoted. After referring to the budget of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) for the fiscal year 1921-22, it observes that Manitoba's share of the taxation contained in that budget, on a basis of her population, is $28,800,000. To that is added interest on the provincial debt, $8,140,000, taxation in the city of Winnipeg, $9,500,000, and also taxation of the municipalities. within the province, $10,750,000, making a total of $57,190,000. It roes on to quote some figures in regard to the cereal crops. I will not weary the committee by quoting them all; but the total value of the cereal crop of Manitoba for that year is shown to be $40,500,000. The paper subtracts this from the total amount of the provincial taxation and interest, and this leaves a deficit of $16,690,000. I do not propose to be an alarmist; but these figures are rather startling when we see that the whole cereal crop of Manitoba in the year 1921 came nearly $17,000,000 short of paying her taxation and interest. It seems to me that the question that we should be considering to-day in all its seriousness is not immigration, but emigration.
I have in my hand a clipping from the Yorkton Enterprise, a paper published in my constituency, and in an editorial in a recent issue, it states':
Although thousands of people have left Canada for the United States during the past *winter, from the self-complacency and indifference exhibited by our legislators at Ottawa-once again ensconced in their magnificent quarters for the transaction of the nation's business-one would imagine that all was well with the country.
Let me say that the handwriting is on the wall for this parliament. This is what the people of western Canada and, I believe, of eastern Canada as well, are thinking of to-day, namely, the problem of emigration, and not that of immigration. From Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island on the east to British Columbia on the west, people are leaving this country in thousands. In a recent newspaper article, I saw the state-(Mr. Campbell.]
ment that fifty families per week were leaving Nova Scotia. I was reading the Charlottetown Guardian a few days ago, and it stated that in twenty years that island had lost all its natural increase and 1,000 of its population per annum in addition. We have not heard very much from Ontario or Quebec as to these conditions; but I noticed that the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers) in his speech a few days ago-this speech was in French and I have just recently read it in English-refers to the very serious emigration from Quebec. There are some illuminating figures in that speech which I would commend to the consideration of some hon. gentlemen in this House.	.
I have a clipping from this morning's paper, a despatch from Windsor, Ontario, dated March 21, which states:
Lured by high wages, hundreds of young Canadians are emigrating to the United States. According to the railway and ferry companies, no fewer than eighty families a day'are entering the States at Detroit.
On one train arriving here this afternoon from the East there were forty-five young men who said they were on their way to Michigan industrial centers. A majority of the men are between 25 and 40 years of age. Most of them came from Toronto, Hamilton and other cities of eastern Ontario. Lack of work and prospect of high wages, they explained, induced them to leave the Dominion. More than half of the 45 are mechanics connected in some way with the building trades.
We come to the prairie provinces again, and tens of thousands of people have left those provinces for the United States. If I might be pardoned for making a brief reference here to another article in the Free Press, it is a report of a meeting of the United Farmers of Manitoba at Elm Creek on November 14. I notice the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) was present at this meeting. The article states:
The president read a letter in which the Hon. D. L. McLeod, provincial secretary, suggested co-operative help from the local for distressed and needy fanners, it being understood that in some districts this year, there are many in need of aid. This subject was freely discussed, and a motion carried that local secretary notify the central organization to the effect that Elm Creek is anxious to help.
When the situation in parts of Manitoba is of sufficient seriousness for the provincial secretary to circularise the locals of the United Farmers of Manitoba, solicting aid on behalf of indigent farmers, surely this is something that should not be ignored and evaded by this House. It seems to me that in considering this situation we are taking a position not much better than that of a certain Emperor of Rome who fiddled while his city was burning. We are playing in this regard a policy of equivocation. I do not want to be understood as opposing a policy

Supply-Immigration

of immigration; I do not understand that any hon. gentleman in this section of the House opposes immigration; but what we do stress is the inadvisability of bringing people to Canada under false pretences. I remember some years ago reading in an English paper an article which told a story of a young English immigrant who had been lured to this country by the tale of high wages on the farm and of how easy it was to start farming. He came to Canada and wandered over the prairies and this eastern country looking for work which he was unable to obtain. Finally he worked his passage back to the Old Country, and almost his first act was to shy a brick through the window of a Canadian immigration office in the city of London. Taken before a magistrate, he told his story and he was allowed to go free, I think rightly. In the western prairies to-day there are thousands of people who are harbouring a sense of injustice, who will feel as long as they live that an injury has been done to them; that they were brought to this country under false pretences. This is a spirit that is poisoning their lives and something that they will pass on to their children. Some of them left much more comfortable homes in the Old Country than they will ever hope to obtain here. Some of them threw up good positions, the like of which they cannot obtain here. We should leave the door open for any good sound, healthy immigrant of a good type who wants to come to this country. Let us invite them here; let them come; but do not carry on a campaign in England, Europe, the United States or anywhere else, because then a distinct responsibility rests upon the government for bringing those people in, very often under false pretences. If we refuse to spend money in this way and let things take their natural course, a considerable number of immigrants will come to Canada and become absorbed without any particular difficulty.
Many hon. gentlemen have stressed the fact that in the period from 1900 to 1913, in which we enjoyed unprecedented prosperity, we were able to absorb a very large immigrant population, and they see no reason why that should not be repeated at the present time. Conditions obtaining at that time do not obtain to-day. We were constructing a third transcontinental railway which opened up millions of acres of good arable free land. The immigrant coming to the country was able to secure, without any particular measure of difficulty, a very good farm adjacent to the railway. He was able to establish his family there in a little cabin in which they lived in fair comfort; then he went out to
work on the railway or in one of the many building gangs that were operating in the country and was able to come back in the fall with a very substantial bank account. In that way he was able to purchase some horses and the necessary machinery and in a short time he became fairly well established on the farm. During that period it is true he was keeping the farm; the farm was not keeping him. But to-day conditions are reversed. The immigrant coming to this country must purchase his land and he has not the privilege of going out and securing work at good wages as in those days. So far, thank Providence, we have had no breadlines in the country; but if a policy of immigration on a vigorous scale were prosecuted we might very easily have those conditions. It is pointed out regularly that by additions to our population we could reduce our debt. That, however, does not always hold good. I can indicate some concrete instances in the West where additions to population by the opening up of new districts have resulted in actually increasing the taxation per head. When a new district is opened up the first few settlers are able to find their way in by wagon trail and there is not much expense. In a little while some more people come in; the roads are fenced off and a highway must be built through a country that is partly timber and partly swamp. This is a very expensive undertaking. The provincial governments are appealed to and a large amount of money is expended on the work. Then a municipality is organized and large sums are borrowed. Later on, come schools, with a borrowing of more money, and still later a branch line, accompanied by the opening of new towns and the building of new elevators, involving further borrowing with increased indebtedness.
The member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who, I am sorry, is not in his seat, has a suggestion to make by way of solving the troubles of the West. He advocated the bringing in of settlers and the building up of industries in the West that would absorb our agricultural products and build up home markets. Is the hon. gentleman aware that in the province of Saskatchewan alone this year we raised six times the amount of wheat that can be consumed by the whole population of Canada, and in the three prairie provinces ten times as much wheat as all the Canadian people would require? In these three provinces the total wheat produced was about
400,000,000 bushels, which would feed 80,000,000 people. Now, supposing that we got 80,000,000 people into the country and that we

started manufacturing industries on a large scale, I would ask my hon. friend where we would sell all those manufactured goods. As to the urgent needs of the country there can be no question. Our public debt is over four and a half billions of dollars, for the federal debt is only a part of the public debt.
One phase of the situation that appears serious to me is the fact that so much of our debt is owed in other countries. Of the Canadian Pacific Railway common stock alone only twenty per cent is held in Canada, and so far as my information goes practically none of their bonds, debentures or preferred stock. It simply means that we are taxing ourselves very heavily, to pay dividends to this corporation, while practically all that money goes out oi the country. It is therefore patent that if we are ever going to get the country on a safe and solid foundation, its basic industry, agriculture, must be placed on a more prosperous footing than at present obtains. "There can be no prosperity", said Sir Wilfrid Laurier, "that does not have its genesis in the soil of our country." The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) suggested the extension of the housing scheme to the farms, and the erection of $2,500 cottages for the use of farm labourers. One of the real difficulties of the farmer in the West, and the hon. gentleman pointed it out himself, is the fact that the farm is already unable to pay its way. I quite agree that the farm labourer is as much entitled to live in a $2,500 cottage as is the worker of the city. But, sir, the farming industry cannot afford to make this possible at the present time. If the government wish to undertake a real colonization policy I am not opposing it; but it will have to be on the basis of financial assistance to the settler. The farmer who comes in and buys land has to struggle against short payments and a high rate of interest, and thousands of these men are being foreclosed on to-day, or, seeing that it is impossible to meet their payments, are moving to the United States or to our cities. It appears to me that if some means were provided by which these men could liquidate the debts with which they are faced to-day, and could have their total indebtedness spread over a period of years at a low rate of interest, thousands of the settlers now leaving Canada could be saved to the country, while on the other hand a great many others could be induced to come in. We hear a great deal about the trek of the young men from the farms to the cities. I think the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) referred to this as the lure of the arc lights. I know

hundreds of young men of that class, and in the great majority of cases they would be only too willing to remain on the farm could they but see any opportunity of owning a farm of their own. But anyone desiring to obtain a farm must pay down a considerable amount of money; and in addition he is faced with high taxation, a short term and a high rate of interest. So that it seems an utter impossibility for him to establish himself. I know that thousands of young men would come back to the farm to-day were they offered an opportunity to purchase farms at reasonably' low rates in districts already settled, and provided their payments were spread over a long term of years at a low rate of interest.
The extension of the Soldier Settlement Board system was advocated by my hon. friend the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) and I heartily agree with him. I think that is the only policy which is possible to-day. It is not a new policy; it has been successfully carried out in New Zealand, and it is the policy that has made Denmark what she is to-day, one of the most prosperous agricultural countries in the world. This policy was tried out with unqualified success in the province of Prince Edward Island. Between the years 1866 and 1875 the province bought out most of the land in the island and re-sold it to the tenant farmers, giving them a long period of years in which to pay and fixing the interest at a low rate, and the history of that policy shows that it re-established the whole agricultural industry in Prince Edward Island.
In conclusion, I want to say that I am not an alarmist, neither am I a pessimist. I have an abiding faith and abounding confidence in the future of western Canada. We have the richest of soil, and in the north we have an abundance of fuel and timber and as well a bountiful rainfall. Nature, indeed, has been most lavish in her gifts. So that with some economic readjustment, with the fiscal changes that must come about if we are to get upon a proper basis of prosperity, and with a sane colonization policy such as has been advocated by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, I have no fear for the future. But, Mr. Chairman, we must shun this false optimism as we would avoid the plague. It was a spirit of this kind that left not only over western Canada, but some years ago also over eastern Canada a path of ruin and destruction in its wake such as we find in the track of a cyclone. Real estate oil and mining booms brought ruin in their train. The people have had enough of them. Ill-founded optimism is

a wily, elusive will-o'-the-wisp that leads not to the high road of prosperity but beckons us further and deeper into the bog and the morass. Let us rather face the future with courage, tempered with caution, taking due note of the handwriting on the wall, paying due heed to conditions around about us, and I have no doubt we shall see a way through.

Mr. Chairman, before the committee took recess I was warned by you that I was liable to get out of order by reading certain statements. I do not wish, of course, to have any disagreement with the Chair, and I will try to limit these statements as much as possible. I think, possibly,. I did not explain sufficiently why I wish to present these statements. If I might refer again to the statement, which I think was made by the minister in Ottawa some time ago, in reference to the difficulty in which the farmer finds himself, I want to show why it is so difficult for the farmer to exist, and to argue from that that the immigrant coming to this country would have a hard job to exist. The reason for that, Mr. Chairman, is this: The farmer is in a class by himself to this extent; he can only purchase what he needs for his living by the products which he raises on his farm, and I was endeavouring, through the statements I was presenting to show that the produce of the farmer had lost in purchasing power compared with ten years ago. One reason why I do that is because the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) said here a few days ago that:
Before the war tariffs were not ruining the West, the West was getting along fairly well; and as soon as the conditions respecting prices, particularly of eastern products, get back where they should be the farmers of the West will prosper, there will be no ruining of the East to help out the West or vice versa.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer hon. members to a statement made in 1911 by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition who was then the member for Portage la Prairie. As reported at page 1931 of Hansard for that year he said:
I do not say that a reduction will, to any very enormous extent, affect the price-
That is the price of agricultural implements.
-I believe it will materially, and I think it will render some relief to, particularly, the farmers of the West, many of whom, notwithstanding any statements that have been made here, are struggling between success and failure every hour.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if many of the farmers of the West were struggling between success and failure some ten years ago I want to try and give this House an idea of the position those farmers must be in to-day. I think

In making this list I have taken from the catalogue to which I referred a similar article in almost every case or if not similar, one as nearly similar as it was possible to find, and I will give you very briefly the purchasing power of a farmer's produce in buying this list of goods in 1912 as compared with 1922. To purchase this list in 1912 would have taken 795 bushels of wheat; today it would take 1,132 bushels. If he purchased this list with the proceeds of his barley it would have taken 1,386 bushels in 1912 and in 1922 it would have taken 2,075 bushels. There is one bright spot in the farmer's market to-day and that is the price of hogs compared with ten years ago. Hogs are now about $2 per hundred pounds higher than they were when I made this list out. Nevertheless it would have taken but 7,520 . pounds of hogs in 1912 to purchase this list of goods whereas in 1922 the amount required would be 9,686 pounds.
I could give some more statements along that line but I do not want to occupy the time of the committee unduly; I simply want to impress upon hon. members the position that the agricultural immigrant is going to be in when he. comes here as Compared with the position which we homesteaders were in ten years ago. If the position is as I have tried to describe it, through the medium of these statements it seems to me that it is economic folly to spend money to bring farmers here under present conditions. Surely no intelligent class of people can be induced to invest their money in agriculture until such times as there is a possibility of securing at least some small return on the investment made. Nevertheless I do not wish to give the committee the impression that the situation is hopeless. We can still produce as much as we ever did and we are willing to do it if we can in turn get our living out of farming. Even if we were producing without a profit, but simply not making a loss, I would be
willing, for my part to go on producing. I do not think it is wise at this time to spend a, lot of money trying to bring immigrants into this country, particularly if it is imperative that they shall be agriculturists. We already have settlers from every country from which we can hope to secure these immigrants; and if you make the people who are now here satisfied, and provide for them better conditions than in the countries from which they came, they will send word back to their friends and we will have a satisfactory flow of emigration from other lands into this country. But we cannot get immigration unless we make conditions better.
The next question which would naturally arise is, how is this to be done? How is the cost of living going to be brought down to where the agriculturist of this country can purchase his living with the produce of his labour? Let me give one example to show how we are suffering from high prices as compared with the price of our own produce. I sold my wheat this year for less than a cent-and-a-half a pound. A few months later I had occasion to buy some rolled wheat and was charged eighteen cents a pound for it. That is a serious condition of affairs surely, when the price for rolled wheat is twelve times higher than the price of the whole wheat itself. Surely it is time for the manufacturers of this country to take some notice of that fact. If I might again quote from Sir John Aird's speech at the annual meeting of the Bank of Commerce:
The cost of our manufactures cannot indefinitely continue to be higher than the farmer and the majority of the consumers in the home market can afford to pay. Not even a revival in foreign trade, unlikely as this appears to be on a large scale in the near future can avail to benefit us if the cost of what we have to sell is higher than in other countries as well or better situated with regard to foreign markets than we are.
He goes on to say that both capital and labour must co-operate in seeing that costs are reduced. It seems to me there is no body of people in Canada who could bring about a reduction in the cost of living so soon as the bankers themselves if they would do it. If they would mete out to the manufacturers of this country the same treatment they mete out to the farmers, we would soon have a reduction in the price of manufactured goods. The banks say to the farmer when he has his wheat produced: You had better sell your wheat and pay off your loan. If the banks would say that to the manufacturer, tell him to sell off his stock of manufactured goods for whatever the market would stand, we would be able to get the goods at a price we could afford to pay. I do not suppose the
