banks will do this because in this country the banks are controlled by the same class of people that control our manufacturing establishments. I am rather afraid that the same set of men are controlling this government, and if that is the case, we shall not get much relief. Possibly I am mistaken: I hope I am. I hope that the government before this session closes will by the legislation it brings down, and particularly the budget, show that it is going to secure for the people of this country a lower cost of living. You will find in the 1919 platform of the Liberal party that they believed a lower cost of living can be secured in this way, because that platform contains this plank:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance: first, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
I would suggest to the minister that he might very well postpone the consideration of these estimates for the Immigration department until after the budget has been brought down. Then we would know whether there was any use spending money trying to get immigrants into this country or not. I am glad he has allowed the second item to stand for some time, and I hope he will see his way clear to postponing consideration of the Immigration estimates until after the budget is down.
There have been so many remarks made during this debate as to the necessity or desirability of filling up the vacant lands in this country that I want to refer briefly to that. I think it is only fair to ask those hon. members who are so anxious to have those vacant lands settled, why they want these vacant lands occupied. Have not the farmers who are here now done pretty well? Is it because we have not produced enough? I have a table here which I would like to present, but I am very much afraid of the Chairman so I will just point out that the production of the farms of Canada last year in grains, field crops, cattle, hogs, sheep and milk totalled SI,399,241,527. You will notice that this does not include fruit and a great many other small items produced on the farms. The value of this production gives no adequate idea of the amount of our production. Let me give just one instance which I have taken from the report of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. It shows that for the year ending March 31, 1921, we exported to the United
'Mr. Coots.]	-
States cattle to the number of 295,000 odd, at a total value of $21,000,000 odd, or an average of S73 per head, and for the year ending March 31, 1922, we exported 172,981 head of cattle to the United States, valued at $3,980,801, making an average of $23 per head. I hope hon. gentlemen will consider what that drop in the value of cattle in one year from $73 to $23 means to the farmers of Canada. Yet hon. gentlemen get up in this House and ask why our farms are mortgaged. What is the reason for that big drop in values? It is because the farmers of Canada are dependent on a foreign market for the price of their products. The hon. member for Fort William dwelt at some length on the value of the home market. I wish to assure the House that we would like very much to have a home market, but we have not got it. We have glutted it so often that no one can blame us for being very skeptical of the ability of the home market to absorb our products. In spite of the fact that we have not got this home market some hon. gentlemen are anxious to fill up our vacant lands. When that is done, what are you going to do with the produce from those lands? That is the question we want answered, and no one in this House has answered it so far in this debate. I have the opinion of an experienced grain man to the effect, that if we had had this year the same average yield of wheat that we had in 1915 the price of our wheat would be 20 cents a bushel less than it is to-day. Some hon. gentlemen will say that that is a very unlikely thing to happen, but let me tell you, on my own farm this year

I happen to live in Alberta-I had a crop of wheat averaging 34 bushels to the acre. I do not believe any hon. member in this House had a better crop. I have no objection to the Acting-Minister of Immigration putting that statement in the literature which he sends out to the countries from which he hopes to get immigrants. I am ready to back it up with my affidavit.

free terms every market that is available. The only foreign market that amounts to much to-day as regards our wheat and cattle is the market in Great Britain. I do not think I need remind the committee that Great Britain to-day is in fairly hard circumstances, because she has an immense debt to pay to the United States; she is largely dependent for her prosperity upon foreign markets, and the markets to which she usually exports much of her goods have had their purchasing power very seriously curtailed on account of the trouble in Europe. I do not wish to stress this point too far, because I think it is an unpopular one. There are in this House many who seem to believe that all we need to do to get prosperity back to Canada is' to produce; but we do not have that example set to us by the manufacturers of this country. When they have produced a little surplus of goods, they lock the door; they tell their workmen to stay away until they get some of those goods sold. The farmer has not done that. The farmer has produced to the very limit of his credit, without any guarantee of even seven per cent dividends, and I do not know of any other class in Canada which has done that. In spite of that fact, the only solution that is offered for our difficulties in Canada seems to be to bring in more farmers to compete with us who are already here, because if you can bring in enough to increase our production of wheat and cattle by 30 per cent, you will succeed only in lowering the price. A gentleman whom I met in my constituency who was a member of the former parliament and who is generally credited with being a hard-headed business man, said to me two years ago: "I do not see why farmers complain so much about so many people leaving the land." He said: "The more that leave the land, the better for the rest of you who are left on it." Hon. gentlemen can easily understand his line of reasoning, and that is the line of reasoning adopted by almost every other class in Canada. That is, they want their own numbers limited, but they want the farmers' numbers unlimited. We have heard a great deal in this country, particularly in the last year and a .half, about class legislation; but I think this proposal is getting very near class legislation.
I have no objection whatever to immigration. I think every man who is a good, moral, physically sound and decent citizen, should be allowed to come into this country; but I do not think people should be brought in here under false representations, and I do not think the efforts of this country should be limited to securing immigrants of one particular class.
That is most unfair. If I were looking at the matter from a strictly farmer's standpoint-and I hope I am not-I would say that what we need in this' country is, not immigration of farmers, but immigration of people who will eat what the farmers are now producing. We can produce; I think we are producing almost enough now in this country to feed 20,000,000 people, and we can produce enough to feed an almost unlimited number. We produced in Alberta this year, although Alberta has a bad name, more wheat than the people of Canada can eat. You must find some place to put that produce, and until you do that, why lay the stress on immigration of farmers? I really cannot see the fairness of this, and more than that I cannot see where much profit is going to come from it.

I presume some hon. member will tell me that we should make butter; but if all the farmers of Alberta go into the dairy business, they can supply Canada with all the butter that she can eat. I do not think the proposition is a hopeless one. I believe, if eVery other class in Canada would do as well as the farmers who are now here are doing and have done for the last five or six years, we would soon return to prosperity in this country. But as I said before, the farmer is the only man who has produced to the limit, put his produce on the market and taken what he could get for it. He has hoarded up no farm produce, and very few farmers have hoarded up any money.
The immigration policy of this country has always been, so far as I have any recollection, directed to bringing into Canada more farmers. We had the soldier settlement scheme

Supply-Immigration

in this country to put soldiers on the land. I always thought that was a little bit unfair to the rest of the soldiers, and I am not going to enlarge on that now. But I want to point out that in Canada we have always laid great stress on production in agriculture. We have spent millions of dollars every year on experimental farms and the promotion of agriculture generally, and the emphasis has always been on production. Practically all our efforts have been directed to greater production, with apparently no effort being made to get us a market.
To keep strictly in order, I want to say just a word or two about retaining people in this country. That has been gone over pretty thoroughly; but one question has not, so far as I know, been touched on, and I want to deal with it very briefly. It is in regard to the people who are leaving this country to get rid of their debts. I know I am on dangerous ground as regards this; but you will find, I think, in the minister's own speech, some reference to a certain percentage of farmers who are bankrupt. Quite a number of our people are leaving this country with the idea that that is the only way in which they can get away from their debts. They know they are bankrupt and that if they stay here and should be able to make some money, it is liable to be garnisheed by their creditors. Under present conditions many men, when they go to a trustee in bankruptcy are advised something to this effect by the trustee:
Before we could undertake to handle an assignment in bankruptcy in this matter, we would have to be advanced the sum of fifty dollars for the payment of preparation of documents, registration and advertising of notices, mailing of notices to creditors and the drawing of statutory declarations. If you are prepared to forward us this amount we shall1, upon hearing from you, send you the papers duly prepared for signature.
The only difference is that some trustees will not accept fifty dollars; they ask seventy-five dollars, or maybe more. The unfortunate part of it is that a great many of these people have not even the $50 to hand to the trustee in bankruptcy in' order to have their assignment taken over by him. I would appeal to the government to- appoint trustees for certain districts, to be paid by the government and to whom a man might make an assignment in bankruptcy if he so desired. I believe that money could be better spent that way than by paying or assisting to pay the passage of some immigrant to this country, because many people who are here already would be glad to remain in the country if they could get some relief from their debts, debts which in many cases have been contracted not through any lack of in-

dustry on the part of these people but more by reason of poor crops, drought and so forth. The minister I think will realize the necessity for something of this kind. I do not know whether he will agree with me that this trustee should be paid by the government, but in any ease I would invite him to consider the point whether it would not be better to spend money in the way I have suggested than in tiying to bring new people to the country. I would call attention to a statement that appeared in the Ottawa Journal last night to the effect that this year's quota of 77,000 immigrants from the British Isles will be exhausted by next month, according to Harry Landis assistant commissioner of immigration at the port of New York. Perhaps it would not be out of place for me to suggest that the minister might arrange with the United States to have all immigrants whom they cannot take in sent here for examination and admittance if they should prove desirable. This article goes on to say that a number of Russian immigrants to the United States have been refused admission, and it might be possible for some of these people to come here if they should prove desirable citizens.
In closing, I would make a suggestion to the government, particularly to the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Fielding) because I think the matter Of success or failure of the farmer immigrant lies very largely in his hands. , I think his success depends upon his having a lower cost of living and access to a larger market than we have at present. The only large market outside our own to which we have free access is that of Great Britain, and I believe that my hon. friend, if he would do his duty, should give Great Britain free access to our market in exchange. That would help the farming industry in this country more than all the other legislation I can think of that could be brought down at the present time. If the Minister of Finance does anything less than this he will not be doing his duty to this country.

Somewhere, Mr. Chairman, I have heard the remark "I had not intended to speak on this subject, but it does seem to me that an item of this kind should not be rushed through the House without discussion." I have no desire to embarrass the minister, because I think he deserves sympathy. It has been suggested that no man in Canada to-day could administer his department with entire satisfaction to this House and to the country. I believe that is correct. I do think, however, that it could be administered with a little more satisfaction to the House and the

Supply-Immigration
country than we have promise of so far. I have a recollection that a wish has been expressed by the minister himself during the progress of the debate that he had some of the qualifications of a noted leader mentioned in Scripture. Most of us will readily recall that when Moses was surrounded by difficulties, amounting in some cases almost to rebellion on the part of his followers, it was a common thing for him to take counsel of his brother Aaron; and when I saw the serious and prolonged conference this afternoon between the minister and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) I wondered whether history was repeating itself. I sincerely hope that this conference between the minister and his political relative once removed, will provide him with that necessary information to enable him to deal with this question with finality next Tuesday.
There is no question that the matter of immigration is of the greatest importance today. This is well demonstrated by the interest that has been evinced in the subject during the course of this debate. I must admit at once that it is a question of such importance that had I the ability, I could not deal with it in the limited time at my disposal to-night However, there are one or two phases of it upon which I wish to touch briefly. Undoubtedly, there is a feeling of nervousness on the part of some interests, and individuals in this country, who take the view that at the present juncture immigration is not desirable in the best national interest. Some have said that owing to Canada's financial situation immigration is not desirable now. This may or may not be true, but I can say without hesitation that, unpleasant as circumstances may be in regard to many lines of endeavour, in regard to many interests and professions in Canada, I still believe that conditions in this country are very much better than they are in any other country in the world, notwithstanding all that has been said to the contrary. There is some apprehension on the part of labour, I believe, that immigration would produce more unemployment, while agriculturists fear that it might result in over-production. The suggestion has also been made to-day that the cause of the trouble is to be found in the tariff. This opens up a large question with which I do not propose to deal. It is possible that my views would not accord with those of some hon. gentlemen in this House, -yet I fancy that if we could wipe out our tariff at one stroke conditions in Canada still would not be anything approaching the millenium. While there have been some objections to immigration, I believe 90J
myself that in the national interest we do need more people to-day, although I am not prepared to say that immigration should be directed entirely toward the farm. I believe Canada is, or is destined to become, a country almost entirely self-supporting. Therefore we need a balanced immigration. Immigration of this kind would be less likely to disturb conditions and lead to the results that some hon. members, evidently fear.
In advancing a few reasons why I personally am not apprehensive in respect to immigration at the present time, may I be pardoned if I mention a few immigrants with whom I have become more or less familiar? During recent years twenty-four immigrants, mostly from the United Kingdom, came here to seek their fortune in a country which they believed provided greater oportunity for their ambition than the Old Land offered. Most of them came without means and without having friends here-practically strangers in a strange land. Yet they have not only made a living, they have prospered to a considerable extent and to-day are in comfortable circumstances, if not in affluence. In adition to that they have been honoured by the constituencies in which they have made their homes, and now ocupy seats in the House of Commons. I should like to know if any one of these twenty-four gentlemen, most of whom are members of the'party seated to my left, will get up to-day and say that the country that has so welcomed and honoured them should now put up the bars and say to the world: No one else need apply; conditions are so bad that we do not fecommend anyone else to come here.

speechtext:
I did not say so. I asked if any of those twenty-four gentlemen would advocate such a policy. However in attempting to answer the question of my hon. friend, I would say that some of the speeches made on this subject sounded dangerously like the advocacy of such a policy. I am willing to admit that conditions are not as bright in Canada to-day with our farmers as we would like to have them. I am willing to go further: I submit that if we in this House attempt to deal with the question of immigration, or with any other question affecting our national interest, it is of the highest importance that we first try to understand, as far as may be possible, the difficulties under
Supply-Immigration

which each section of the country labours. There can be no satisfactory solution of the problem so long as we each feel that the other party in interest does not know what he is talking about. This question must be approached in the same spirit as all other national questions-a spirit of compromise and sympathy.
I have heard during the course of this debate and in other debates too, a great deal about the wonderful natural resources possessed by this country. Undoubtedly we are greatly blessed in this respect. But, Sir, is there any possible way in which we can even approach the proper development of these vast natural resources without a greater population than we have at present? As this question affects our farmers, let me say there are two opportunities open to men engaged in any line of production, and particularly to farmers. In order to make farming profitable we must secure wider and better markets, or else lessen our cost of production. I believe that the prospects for higher prices in the near future are not very bright. Therefore it is up to us by all means possible to reduce our production costs. I know that in my own section-and surely the same condition must apply to the West-if we had more men on the land wages should be a little lower, resulting in a little lower cost of production than has obtained during the last three or four years. So viewed from any angle a properly balanced immigration should be beneficial to Canada.
There may bp a difference of opinion as to how we should proceed to secure such immigration. Personally I believe an immigration policy to be effective should not be spasmodic but should be a steadily continued policy conducted along sound lines. I think the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) stated in answer to a question that about $269,000 was to be expended this year in advertising. At the moment I do not propose to question the wisdom of this expenditure, but I want to point out a factor that I think is vitally necessary and supplemental to advertising, and that is to see that the quality of our goods is such that our customers will continue to purchase. In other words, no government should attempt to deal with this important question of immigration without bearing in mind these two aspects, each complementary to the other, namely, the desirability of attracting immigration; and the retention of the immigrants so attracted. To attempt to deal with immigration from the one angle alone is in my judgment simply an admission of incompetence. I have a high opinion of

the energy of a man who attempts to fill a bottomless pail with water, but a mighty poor opinion of his judgment. Therefore, I believe it is the duty of the government before attempting to stimulate immigration to study first the conditions which cause the loss of immigrants after they reach our shores. Nc doubt in all countries immigration is accompanied by a certain amount of emigration; and while Canada has suffered from emigration in the past, still I believe lately we have been losing in greater proportion than is consonant with our national welfare. Therefore, while I do not wish to depreciate the value of advertising, no money spent upon it at the present time can compare in results with the money spent on a stamp that carries to the Old Land a letter from a satisfied immigrant. A satisfied customer in this, as in all other businesses, is the best advertisement.
Now, in my judgment this question should be handled entirely by the minister and his department, and not by private enterprise.
I have not a great deal of faith in a combination of the two. I have seen the results of immigration to this country due to private enterprise. Circulars depicting conditions in the most glowing colours were distributed in Great Britain and other countries and a very desirable class of immigrants was attracted here, but they were settled in localities where success was practically an impossibility, and the main welcome extended to them was a scramble to relieve them of surplus cash under the guise of supplying them with necessary equipment. They were, in short, bled white by the very speculators who brought them here. The advertising that that class of settler distributes from this country is of the most damaging kind.
There is another class of advertising, of which I speak, perhaps, with some reluctance. We have had during last session and this, a kind of advertising distributed throughout this House and the country by the representatives of the people. I do not for a moment doubt the truth but I do very much question the wisdom of it. I do not know how any country or any business could make a success if in connection with it the kind of advertising was carried on that we have distributed in the last year and a half. If I were engaged in a business, which, as it likely would be at this time, was labouring under financial difficulty, I would not send out salesmen at a salary of $4,000 a year to proclaim everywhere my financial condition, and then have any hope of surviving. I am in sympathy with those who are subject to the conditions that I believe exist in the West, but I am not

Sup ply-Immigration
in favour of .publishing our family troubles to the world, because I believe, as I said at the beginning, that conditions in other countries are worse than they are in Canada. The vital need of the Canadian people to-day is a little more faith in themselves and their country, and an inclination to dwell a little more on the bright spots than is the case at present.
We have heard some very doleful tales with respect to conditions in the West and also in other parts of Canada, but I am sure that we could at the same time make public accounts of outstanding successes on the part of farmers in all sections of the country. I am willing to admit that conditions may not be as good now as they were formerly, but surely in this great country, with all the resources it has, it is not the part of wisdom, it is not the part of good business or good judgment, to advertise to the world that we are in the deplorable condition that some hon. members feel impelled to portray to the committee. There are certain conditions which may accelerate this movement of people from our borders, and it should be the duty of the government to study the whole question from every angle and attempt to apply a remedy. I venture to suggest that if by the exercise of stringent economy there could be a slight lessening of the burden of taxation resting upon the people to-day; if there could be even a small surplus reported by the hon. the Minister of Finance, it would be a hopeful sign that would do a great deal to attract attention to us and bring us a most desirable class of immigrants.
I am not, Sir, a believer in immigration attracted by over-coloured advertising, because that kind- of inducement appeals to a class of people-unfortunately, to be found in almost every country-who wish to get rich quickly, who wish to get something for nothing. . The class of people we want in this country, the ones who will do the most good, are those who come without capital, if you wish, or better still, with capital, but with plenty of ambition and a determination to work and to succeed. There is room in this Dominion for thousands, yes, for millions of that class of people. Many of them have come to our shores in the past and have succeeded here and contributed a great deal to the building up of our nation, and still more could be accommodated. We need therefore a policy of immigration not based on financial exploitation-or corporationist greed -but rather do we need a national policy based on sound business principles and having
in view the best interests and requirements of Canadian citizenship.

I am not going to say that the farmers of Ontario are doing a great deal of grumbling about immigration, but a certain amount of immigration can be used to advantage in that province. They need help on the farm. In some cases it would not be necessary to build houses for the help because on a great many farms in Ontario that are being pastured there already exist empty houses and good houses at that. There is no question about it that the farmers in Ontario to-day cannot get help. On the , Toronto train recently I met a neighbour of mine who was going down to the city to hunt for a man. I saw him in town afterwards and asked him how he had made out. "Well," he said, "I got one man who promised to meet me at the station; I am not sure whether he will be there or not. The rest all told me that they would go to the farm just when they could get nothing else to do. They were going to stay in the city a while longer and see if they could not get something there before they would go to the farm."
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am going to say something with which I do not think the committee will agree to the extent they agreed with my first statement. I concur in a great many things that have been said as to what is wrong with agriculture-that is high freight rates, the tariff, and a lot more things are responsible for present conditions. But I am going to mention one thing, which has not yet been mentioned and which may not be popular in this House; nevertheless I think it is time that somebody said it and I am going to be the one. That is one of my reasons for taking part in this debate. Along with other things that are wrong my opinion is that we have too many people in Canada to-day who think that Canada owes them a living. I believe that Canada owes a living to the returned men who are disabled and their dependents; that is one of the responsibilities the war has brought upon us. But I claim that outside of that class Canada owes no man a living who is able to work; it does owe every man a chance to make an honest living. The trouble is we have a class of people in this country who want to work shorter hours for more pay. If a farmer goes to work with his team on the roads he can get $5 a day for himself and his team. He supplies the team, the wagon and the harness. He furnishes the grease for that wagon, board' the team, Repairs his harness, and furnishes the whole outfit for $5. He also has to board

himself as well as the team. ' Now, if the chimney blows off his house in a storm and it is necessary for him to get a bricklayei to rebuild that chimney he or his man will have to work with the team, and he will have to board that team and himself, and perhaps his help, for two days in order to pay the bricklayer for a day's work in rebuilding that chimney.
I believe in every person getting a chance to make an honest living. I do not believe, as some do in bringing in immigrants to compete with the farmers in order to produce more potatoes and thus make potatoes cheaper and at the same time keep out artisans for fear they may bring down the wages of plasterers, bricklayers, or other mechanics in this countiy. I believe it was the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), who said there were 6,000 unemployed in Winnipeg and therefore we should not bring in any more immigrants. If the present conditions continue we will always have unemployed in Winnipeg and other large centres. If the present Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization is going to wait until we have no unemployment in Winnipeg, or other cities, before he makes a move he wdl have to wait until our population is only one-half of what it is at the present time, and perhaps longer. I think the government can change the existing conditions, although I will not dwell on that point at the present moment. The people themselves can change the conditions if they are willing to go to work, but we do not want immigrants who want to live without working. I was surprised to hear even some of the hon. members on this side complaining. When I look at the hon. members from the western provinces in whose ranks I sit I observe practically that one-half of them were immigrants. I think we can also put in that category three premiers of the western provinces. Now, if a carefully selected immigration policy has provided Canada with men of that type, I think that policy has done a great work for this country.
Now as to the class of people that we want, a case was brought to my attention not long ago. A young American came over to a town near the border, between here and Toronto, and rented a garage shop. He paid three months' rent in advance in order to secure the shop and then returned to the other side in order to make his arrangements. This happened last winter. He went back home and packed up his belongings and started with his wife for Canada. But when he got to the border he found that he could not be ad-

Supply-Immigration
mitted unless he would sign a statement that he was a farmer. This he absolutely refused to do because he was an honest man; he declared he knew nothing about farming. The matter was discussed for two weeks, from December 28 until January 10, and then the Immigration department decided to let him enter the country. By that time, however, he had gone back home and started a garage shop there. I think that man would have made a good citizen. In my opinion we might have admitted him to Canada; his entrance into the business might have brought down the price we have to pay for getting our cars fixed.
What do we need to-day in order to boost our cities and towns? We have heard a great deal about the value of the home mai'-ket; it has been mentioned several times in this debate. It reminds me of a story I heard about a woman who had six boys. She said her boys all made money on a wet day trading in old clothes with each other. The old clothes were all in the family in the morning and they were all in the same family at night. If we consume all we produce how are we going to pay our liabilities abroad and keep out of debt? What is necessary in order to make our towns prosperous-and I think the business people in the cities and towns have not yet realized it-is this: You want a contented industrious Canadian citizen on every one hundred acres around each town in the province of Ontario. As the result of such a policy the business men in those towns will do better, and the manufacturers, the wholesale men in the large cities will ship more goods to those towns, and the whole country will be benefited thereby.
A great deal has been said about our natural resources. We have those resources and we are very proud of them. But if you take a ton1 of coal from a coal mine you have reduced your natural resources to that extent; if you cut down a tree our forest resources have been reduced by that much; if you take a fish from the ocean, lake or stream, our fishery resources are to that degree lessened; but when you produce from the land, provided your farming is properly conducted, you have not diminished nature's storehouse to any appreciable extent. Therefore what is necessary, as I said before, is to get farmers on every one hundred acres, or you might make it one hundred and sixty acres in the West.
The farmers have not much to do. They only have to clothe and feed and shelter the people of the world-that is all. I said I would not speak for more than ten minutes and my time is about up. How can we help
in these conditions? I would say first, that we should relieve the agriculturist of the heavy burden he is carrying at the present time by taking off his back the plutocrat and the profiteer. Mr. Chairman, this is not the wail of an infant industry for protection which we have heard so often in this House. This is an appeal, and an appeal from the mother of industries, that she may be relieved of those whining infants that are clinging to her skirts and have grown bloated. Remove them, and you will help her to recover. I have faith in agriculture. I have faith that she will soon recover, and more than that, I have faith that she will assist the Finance Minister in paying not only the interest on our national debt, but in paying off that debt.
Another thing about which we should think very seriously is this: The time has come, yea, I might say it has passed when the people of this country should live within their revenue. I would go a step further and say that the time has come when the government of this country should live within its revenue. I am a believer in this country. I believe in Canada. I have not lost faith yet.
It has been said that the minister might tell the immigrants whom he hopes to induce to come to this country what they are coming to. I would not like him to tell them all. He might tell the. immigrant that he wants to have come out here from the Old Country that we have a heavy debt and want him to help pay it. But do not tell the immigrant's wife that if her husband happens to die she will have to pay a tax on the rough lumber that goes into his coffin. Do not tell her that she will have to pay a tax on his shroud. Do not tell her that she will have to pay a tax on the screw nails that fasten down the coffin lid, and that the man who digs the grave will also have to pay a' tax on the shovel he uses for that purpose. Do not tell the immigrant that if his wife should have to make a living by sewing, before she can earn five cents to buy a loaf of bread with, she will have to pay a tax of $13.05 on her sewing machine. Do not tell her that if she has to earn her living by washing she will have to pay a tax in Canada on the washing machine she uses. The minister had better keep these things from them. But he might incidentally let them know that in a few years we may have a Progressive government in this House that will take that tariff off.

It might at least inspire them to endeavour to acquire that feeling of contentment to which the hon. member for North Ontario referred when he said "What we v'ant is a contented and industrious man on every hundred acres!" Contentment does not come because, a man has so much goods; contentment comes from work largely and from some internal qualities that are not supplied by government. If the men who come out here learn to take what comes to them until they find their feet, they will be an asset to this country just as our fathers were. As regards everybody on this side and most hon. members over there, if they are not immigrants themselves their fathers were. My father was an immigrant; he came out here when he was a young man of nineteen, and nearly everybody in Canada has sprung from stock that came out here as young men to seek their fortunes and to establish themselves in Canada. They have established themselves in Canada. But this everlasting protest against competition is something that we must take account of only to disregard it, and that is the position I take about the matter. speechtext: The men who do not mind that are no good. There may be some who do not mind that; but if a man has any tittle of self respect in him, he will mind it. The point I am trying to make is this: If the farmer classifies himself in comparison with the artisan, then I say he is a long way better off than an artisan. If he classifies himself with a business man, he is better off than most business men. Farmers think it is an easy thing to go into business and succeed, and they try it sometimes. I have known many men who have sold their farms, worth ten or twenty thousand dollars, and have gone into business where they would have a nice time, just buying and selling. It is so easy to buy so much at such a price and to sell it at so much more, and the record of failures contains the names of hundreds and thousands of men just like those. It is not every man who is fit for business, and even those who are fit for business have difficulties to overcome and problems to solve. They keep those to themselves for the sake of their credit, as the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Stansell) said, but many sleepless nights are caused thereby. The business men of this country have just as much to contend with as our farmers have.

subtopic: QUESTIONS AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS-QUESTIONS AND THEIR ANSWERS
speechtext: Does the hon. member know of any business men who have made a success of business, who have gone on to a farm and made a failure?

subtopic: QUESTIONS AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS-QUESTIONS AND THEIR ANSWERS

If the hon. member will come to the neighbourhood of the city where I live, I can show him many business men who have undertaken to do farming. Some of them have succeeded and some have not. This depends altogether on the man, and it depends altogether on the man whether he
is a good or a bad farmer. If he is a good farmer, he will be successful, and if he is not, he will not. A few years ago, we had a very interesting committee on the cost of living. We had many distinguished men giving evidence, and that committee had a series of stock questions which they submitted. Dealing with agriculture particularly, the witnesses were asked in every case: "Now what is the principal factor in making a success of dairying, stockraising?" and so on. The invariable answer was: "The man." That is the principal factor. We had in the town of Belleville a man running a dairy and making so much money that he asked us not to make him expose the fact. He was taking his cream from Renfrew where a co-operative dairy was running which had never paid a dividend in its lifetime. The man is the factor, and my hon. friends to my left and their friends in Ontario, who think it is an easy thing to go into business and to make a great deal of monqy, have had their experience in Ontario. If my information is correct, they are gaining some experience purchasing it at somewhat higher prices. Even out on the prairies, some of the co-operative schemes have not panned out because of the fact that the men who are trying to run them are not good business men. To be a good business man one must have capacities that are not found on every farm or in the mind of every artisan.
I was interested and somewhat amused at the speech delivered by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). He painted a very gloomy picture. Things were bad because the crop was not big. and even if the crop was big, things would not be any better! Even if all the farmers got 34 bushels of wheat to the acre, that would not make any difference to them; they would not be any better off! That is not the kind of talk we should bear in parliament, and to my mind that is somewhat stupid. Anyone who argues that a man with a good crop cannot make any more than a man with a poor crop, has no basis at all upon which to stand; but that is the argument the hon. member put up.
My hon. friends do not want farmers to come out. The Trades and Labour Council do not want artisans to come out. I believe we ought to have more artisans come to Canada. I believe every man who comes out here creates a demand for the goods that are made by other people, and if hon. members want proof of that, let us take the experience and the prosperity of Ontario farmers adjacent to good-sized towns. Some of my hon. friends flouted the home market. The home market is the most valuable thing an agricul-
Supply-Immigration

turist can have. I was down recently in the county of Prince Edward, and there is not a poor man in the whole county. They have only a few towns but they grow stuff for canning, and that makes them all prosperous. Without the canning factories established there,-those Dominion Canners' factories, about which my hon. friends eompiain so much at times-the farmers of that county would not have the prosperity they are enjoying. I could take my hon. friends to counties in western Ontario in which are situated good-sized towns or small cities, and there they will find men, with ordinary degrees of intelligence, not only making a splendid living, but putting away a competence through their work on the farm. Farming is hard work, I admit, but it is not as hard as working in a factory. The farmer can work twelve hours outdoors more easily than an artisan can work eight or ten hours indoors and without so much loss of health and strength.

I will give you a chance if my hon. friends opposite are willing. In my judgment the best thing that can be done is to encourage the immigration of farmers, f think that farmers ought to be encouraged to come to Canada because there are millions of opportunities for farmers here, as compared with any other class of the community. There are millions upon millions of acres of unoccupied lands, in the country, and what other class of people could we induce to come who would have such an opportunity of making a living and a competence as those men whom we could put on the farms? I think therefore that this is the right class. I believe, however, that a substantial number of artisans should also be induced to come into the country and that this could be done to the general advantage of the people. One of the ways of doing that is in my judgment to improve every possible means of transportation. I can tell my hon. friends that the immigrants who come in to take up land in competition with them will obtain a greater advantage from the improvement of the transportation system than they will in any other direction. I should like to see the Vancouver and the St. Lawrence routes improved and the Hudson Bay railway built, not because I think it would be a good thing, but because I think it is necessary, to allay the dissatisfaction that exists in the West, to spend that money and demonstrate that the thing cannot be done. .
By every other conceivable means we ought to make it possible for the men who come
here as immigrants to have that much better chance of making not only a living but a competence within a reasonable period of time. Half the members here already have a competence. There are men sitting on this side of the House who have made a competence in a few years. My hon. friend from North Ontario is a retired farmer. You can go into towns all over Canada and find retired farmers by the dozen. But you do not find many retired business men, you do not find retired artisans. The farming industry is the only one that enables a man to retire unless he has a bee in his bonnet and starts into business, in which event he would soon have to retire to the poorhouse. But so long as he takes care of the money he made in agriculture to keep him in his old age he will be happy and contented and go down honoured and mourned into that wooden box which my hon. friend from North Ontario spoke of-and it will be the last tax he will ever have to pay!

Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting for four days for an opportunity to speak, and have been getting hoarser and hoarser listening until now I can scarcely articulate. Therefore I feel quite gratified that I have the opportunity before I become any worse. I feel that I should almost offer an apology to the committee for attempting to speak to-night, but I shall do my best to make every one hear me, although I do not know whether I shall succeed.
During the course of this debate I have listened to a great deal that I approve of and a great deal that I doubt whether it was wise to have uttered. But at the same time I do not feel that as a member of parliament I should be restrained in saying what I conscientiously believe, so I am not going to question what any hon. member has already said on the subject of immigration. I am an immigrant myself, Mr. Chairman.

I did not come to this country until I was forty-one years old. I had a family growing up and did not feel that where I lived I was getting ahead sufficiently to provide the kind of home that I wanted my children to enjoy, and I found that year by year it was becoming more difficult to realize my ambition. Therefore I looked around for some place where with energy and the exercise of what common sense I possessed I could get ahead and lay up sufficient to guarantee my children a home. I have done that in Canada, and I do not feel that Canada has treated me so badly, although be-
Supply-I immigration

fore this House last year I expressed the opinion that after living twenty-five years in my constituency it was amazing to me to see some people in the deplorable condition they were in at that time. Now, last year was the poorest I ever saw in that district, although we had enough for thepeople to eat and enough for our stock. But a country with a record like that for twenty-five years, harvests year after year that provided plenty for man and beast, is not a very bad country to live in. However, we must make conditions that will enable the average man and woman to make good and secure a living on the land, for after all the dearest thing to every man or woman is a home. I think every industrious person should be entitled to acquire a home free from encumbrances-a home that is actually his or her own. All people in my district, I am sorry to say, have not been able to accomplish that. It is only fair to say that they have been handicapped by artificial conditions, which should have been and could have been altered for their amelioration, to some extent by the government, and to a greater extent by the people themselves if . they had only seen it that way. And it may be added that during the war we learned to live so expensively that we are not willing to return to the old way again, but I think we have got to do so whether we like it or not.
I do not believe there is a man or woman anywhere in the world who is more entitled to possess a good home than the farmer and his wife. I do not believe there is any more useful couple in this world and a couple more needed at the present time than the farmer and his wife. Consequently I should like to see it made possible for them to be prosperous, and thus bring prosperity to Canada. In my opinion the government could go a long way towards helping along this line. Many opinions have been pronounced on this point, and I expressed my own pretty fully last year, so I shall not repeat them tonight, but I want the government to understand that the people are holding them responsible to do all that it is humanly possible for a government to do to help make the country prosperous at this time.
I have tried to learn to be practical. Now, I know that we are a party to debts that we must pay or repudiate. Once we understand that, then we must act with reason and with common sense. We have natural resources that we are unable to use because there are not enough people here to develop them. Members all over this House say they are not opposing immigration, that they are willing that people should come in. I go further

and say that I want to see a reasonable and. forceful immigration policy brought into effect.
I say that because I believe all our troubles can be better solved with more people here than they can be with the number we have now. The bringing in of more people and the ameliorating of our difficulties through the application of remedies must go hand in hand.
I say to my hon. friends, with the best intentions, that I believe they have gone too far in telling of the difficulties in the West. There is.no doubt that these difficulties exist, but they are not to be overcome in a day, in a year, or perhaps even in my lifetime. I want to do what I can to assist in overcoming them, but I do not go so far as to say what some hon. members have said, namely, that we must fix things up here before we can bring people into the country. I believe that to bring people here will help us. fix things up. I would not go at that work, however, without a conscience. I claim to have a conscience in this matter, and I submit that we can invite people to come to Canada in the full knowledge that there are undeveloped resources here for them to work with and that they will r.ot need to take those resources out of our possession in order to make good.
There are many hon. members who are afraid of the competition that will be created by those who are brought into the country. Well, I am in favour of having people brought here who are likely to become good Canadian citizens so that they may co-operate with us and help us pay our debts and become a prosperous nation. I would rather do that than say that would-be immigrants must stay out until we get rid of all our difficulties. If I thought that people who come here would not have an opportunity to make good I would not like to ask them to come. When I first came here I was offered so much per head-I did not know very well what it involved at that time-to bring people into the country. I was not willing to do it, because I ddi not know whether or not the people who came in would be able to make good. But having been this long in the country I know something about the natural conditions and I know they are good enough to enable people to be successful. We have problems to solve, and those who come in can help us solve them. I know what the conditions are both in Canada and in the United States. I spent a good many years in the United States; I have relations living there, and I am in close touch with what is going on. It is my opinion that many people who are going to the United States will be glad to come

Supply-Immigration
back here if we do what we can to alleviate our present difficulties. They will find out that Canada is the best place on
10 p.m. this earth for anyone who wants to have a home of his own; that he can get it more easily and more quickly here than he can anywhere else in the world. Many people are going to the United States, I know, but they are not going on farms; in fact, they could hardly buy farms there, considering the prices that lands are being held for. Our land in Canada is just as good as the land in the United States; at least, it is in the part of the country in which I live-* and I know of the conditions in the United States because I have been from east to west and as far south as Mexico. Hon. members will agree, therefore, that I know what I am talking about.
It will take a lot of money in salaries for immigration agents to offset what we have heard in this House during the last few days. If hon. members want to make those statements, if they want to deliver speeches of that kind, I am willing that they should do so; I am not trying to control them. But so far as their statements go about the conditions that prevail, I am not going to rest easily until I tell you, Sir, that the conditions are not as bad as that in the constituency that I represent. They may be bad artificially, but the natural conditions, the soil and the climate in the district where I live, are equal to those in the country in which I used to live a thousand miles to the south. Most people are afraid of the winters out in that country. Well, it is my experience that the winter at Edmonton is easier to stand than the winter in Nebraska or Iowa where I lived most of the time before I came here.

Ottawa just now. I do not intend to talk about any part of the country that I am so little conversant with that I do not know what I am talking about.
I repeat Mr. Chairman, that I have faith in Canada. Canada is going to come out all right, but we may have to put Progressives on the other side of the House before we get things right. I hope our men will agree and work together until we can impress upon Canada the need of the changes that we have been asking for. There are several things that the farmers in the West need, and I judge they are needed in the East as well. One thing we must do is to live cheaper. We must be able to buy cheaply what we need to buy.
But before going further I want to say this. I know of farmers living in the West who are buying practically all they need for their subsistence. They do not even cultivate a garden; they do not have a cow or pigs to furnish them with meat. And when a farmer is trying to carry on farming without a garden, or a cow, or pigs it does not look very good to me.

I was saying that farming without a garden, without a cow, without pigs does not look very good to me. Yet that is what is going on in some districts and it is not the right way to farm. My parents lived in Ohio a long time ago and raised wheat until the soil was so impoverished that wheat growing could no longer be successfully carried on; then they raised a crop of a different character. Later the family went into Iowa and grew wheat there until they could no longer make a success of it and had to turn their attention to raising something else. When I was ten years old I went with my father into Nebraska and we'did the same thing there; we raised wheat as long as we could do so successfully, and then had to turn our attention to other crops. I do not think the raising of wheat can be regarded as a permanent agricultural operation, nor do I think that a man engaging in farming as a mere business proposition without any idea of making a home for himself, is a very good farmer. I think that to be considered a good farmer a man needs to go on to a piece of land with the intention of making a home there, of establishing there a place to live in and enjoy life. Mr. SU1HERLAND:	I may say that I
do not feel as keen to speak on this question now as I did about a week ago when the matter was first brought before the House. After listening to the many speeches which have been delivered I am very glad indeed, as I am sure are the majority of the members of this House, that the hon. member for Strat.h-cona (Mr. Warner) in spite of the difficulty under which he labours at the moment has endured until the end almost, and delivered the speech which he did here tonight. I think that it is much to his credit that he has spoken in the way he has. I have wondered often as I listened to the remarks which were delivered in this debate if the speakers appreciated the effect of the words which fell from their lips, and the thought flashed on my mind that we were inclined to forget in this parliament sometimes that we were the representatives, not of a particular constituency or of a particular class, but that every member of the House of Commons was here representing the Dominion of Canada.
As I listened to some of the objections which were raised against the bringing in of immigrants to this country, that it was going to encroach bn someone's prerogatives, I thought as I viewed in my mind this vast expanse of territory which we have here with only a few millions of people endeavouring to occupy and develop it, what claim can we advance to justify our monopolizing all these broad acres and all the undoubted resources which this country possesses if there is a congestion in some other part of the world? Surely this is not in keeping with the policy that some of those who objected so strenuously to immigration have been advocating.
I shall not attempt to cover the whole range of subjects that have been touched on in this debate, but there are some features which did appeal to me as requiring some further explanation from the minister and the government. I was not at all surprised that considerable opposition to this policy came from the government benches, and some also from both groups on this side of the House. The question of immigration under present conditions is a very serious and a very vital one to the future welfare of this Dominion. It is, as I think has already been acknowledged by some members of the government, perhaps the most important and vital question that can engage the attention of the government
Supply-Immigra tion

and of parliament at the present time. I appreciate the difficulties which the minister and the government have to contend with in this matter, and the pressure that is being brought to bear from so many different sources. I believe that any hon. member of this House, if he was left free to act according to his best judgment, would adopt a very different policy from the one that has been placed before us for bringing immigration to this country. I think the policy is narrow and sectional, but it is possibly in keeping with the age in which we are living and the times through which we are passing. I sometimes wonder if the whole world has not gone mad, if something is not necessary to bring people to their senses. It is just possible that the best thing we could experience at this time would be a period of very severe depression in order to bring people back to their senses.
Surprise is expressed in some quarters that the youth of our country are not remaining where they were born and brought up. I do not think any surprise should be exhibited at this at all, because they are the sons of a colonizing race. This is evidently bred in the bone, and one can hardly expect that people of this disposition are going to remain in the place where they were born and brought up, notwithstanding how ideal conditions there may be. We have in Canada the descendants of two great races, and we all believe that we have in this Dominion a great country and that we are going to become a great people. I often wonder if the fact that people of French descent are more inclined to remain at home and not to wander so far abroad is not due to the circumstance that they are not the descendants of a race that has been so historically noted for its colonising proclivities. The Anglo-Saxon has wandered all over the world, and wherever there was a vacant place, you could rest assured he was there, establishing the Union Jack. This is going on to-day, and notwithstanding the fact that many of our young men are going to the United States at the present time, I am sure, as the hon. member for Strathcona has already said, that you will find them trooping back again in the course- of a few years, if we only do our duty by ourselves under present circumstances. It is an easy mat~ ter at any time to find fault with a government which has to carry on, and it is very easy to find fault with the present government. I am inclined sometimes to wonder why many of the things which we heard about during the general election which took place a couple of years ago, have evidently [Mr. Sutherland.I '
been forgotten and why no effort has been made to put those policies into effect, if they were going to prove to be such a benefit for our country. I am not, however, going to blame the government for that, because I believe it is in the public interest that they should forget those old platforms of theirs, which they did not take very much stock in themselves, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has several times intimated to the House.
To my mind, the one outstanding matter which is affecting those particularly engaged in agriculture to-day is the enormous quantity of imported produce that is being disposed of in the Canadian market. I noticed the ex-president of the Ontario Agricultural College, Dr. George Creelman, in a speech which he delivered in Toronto a few months ago, stated that last year $168,000,000 worth of farm produce was imported into this country.
I am referring to this matter for the benefit of some of my hon. friends to the left who think that some remedy different from the one I propose, should be applied to our difficulties.
But there are other matters that I should like to touch upon, and I am going to point out very briefly the greatest difficulty which we have to encounter at the present time and the one which possibly, above all others, is responsible for our present condition. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) referred to the need of competition in order to have proper development. I believe that is the case; when you eliminate competition, you are going to injure somebody in the process and you are going to remove the incentive which is necessary to bring out the best there is in anyone. That rule applies, it does not matter where you go, and one of the most serious things that we have had to face during the past few years is the fact that we have, not' only in this Dominion, but in practically every other country, what is known now as organized labour. They have in several instances dictated to the rest of the people of this country who might be termed as labourers more than they in several respects. The effect during the present winter of the attitude of organized labour in connection with the mining of coal has been almost a calamity to this country. It has indeed, been so serious that it has overreached any temporary benefit which they have received, and those who have suffered most have been the wage-earners of Canada. The same thing, I believe, applies with regard to our transportation facilities. The unions took control of the railways of this country during the war period, and they

Supply-Immigration
absolutely made it impossible for the railways to be operated so that the best interests of the country could be served. I point to those as two illustrations to show what happens when competition is eliminated and matters are regulated in that way. This means simply that you have to organize every class upon a similar basis if you are going to put them on an equal footing, and if you do that you are right back again where you started.
As regards the idea that by having the people of this country divided into sections and classes, if you are going to reap a temporary advantage, that can be done only by injuring some other class which is not so well organized as the class which is receiving a temporary benefit. The effect of this is that eventually you get back exactly to where you started. I hope, before we have to go through that whole process, something will be done to stop that course and to make the people realize that the government are going to act on behalf of all the people of this country, regardless of whether they are an organized body or not and able to bring influence to bear upon the government.
A year ago, as I listened to the Minister of Finance during the budget debate, when he was pointing out how he had made certain reductions on some things, I wondered if that was because of the pressure which had been brought to bear, and if no reductions had been made on other items because no pressure had been brought to bear. I merely mention that to show the effect an organized body will have in bringing influence to bear upon the government. I am afraid this is the very thing the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) encountered in endeavouring to bring about an immigration policy to serve the interests of this country. As I listened to the statements he made on several occasions during the debate which is taking place, he virtually admitted that he was not attempting to do much; in fact, several of his supporters charged him with not having a policy at all. He scarcely claimed that this was a policy; but he was following the line of least resistance, and he hoped to get through in that way. I am afraid such a course will not suit present conditions in this country. I know, as regards the province from which I come, we do not want to steer a middle course by which we shall be subject to the least criticism. What should and what must be done is to meet the demands of this country, and anyone who says that there is no need of more labour in this country; that we have many people out of employment and that until they are absorbed, more people must not be brought
into this country, is losing sight of the fact that there are thousands and tens of thousands of opportunities in Canada, works thar ought to be carried on that are standing still to-day because there are not enough people here to carry them on. The farmers of Ontario are only half farming; they are not doing anything like what they could or would like to do, owing to the fact that there is no labour available.
Why is there not labour available? It is simply because the labour from the farm goes into the towns where there are abundant opportunities and where wages are much higher than they are in the rural districts. Someone may ask why that is the case. Well, let me tell you what happened a short time ago. Mr. Tom Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Congress, went to Toronto and insisted that the provincial government adopt an eight-hour day for certain classes who were working on government contracts, and that they should pay a minimum wage. This was to apply to all classes of labour except farmers. When he was asked why he did not extend this provision to farm labour he said that this class of labour was in the nature of a family affair and should not come under these regulations. Now, we as a parliament are responsible for fixing the hours-of labour for the servants of the people. We were the guilty parties in the first instance in fixing the hours of labour of those engaged in the Civil Service much below the standard of people engaged in any other walk of life. Is it any wonder that others look to us as setting an example of what might be accomplished by organization and pressure? It is generally recognized that the farmer cannot carry on under these conditions, and this has been demonstrated on many occasions. When we adopted daylight saving in this country there was a vigorous protest from the farmers, because undoubtedly it hampered them and made it much more difficult for them to get the necessary labour on the farm. The very fact that agriculture is languishing as it is today, particularly in western Canada, owing to the many difficulties with which it has to cope, shows that an abundance of labour is the only thing that can solve the problem. I called the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) during this session, to one article which I thought should be exempt from the sales tax for the reason that there is absolutely no labour to be had in the province of Ontario in connection with its production. And although we may not hear very much of an outcry, nevertheless there is

an insistent demand on the part of the farmers for something to be done in this direction.
The minister (Mr. Stewart) said that so far as Ontario was concerned, the province preferred to keep its office in London and engage in practically the same work as is carried on by the federal government in bringing immigrants to the country. Do the government and the House consider that it is fair to the province of Ontario that it should have to do work of this kind in this way? A number of years ago the federal government undertook to make a disposition of all the immigrants coming into Canada, and the Ontario government gave up the work in which they had been engaged. Ontario was practically neglected because nearly all, in fact one might say all, the literature published and, circulated by the Department of Immigration for years back has been devoted to western Canada, while little or none has been published to serve the purposes of that province. The publications issued by the Department of Agriculture itself, which are in the greatest demand by well-informed people in the Old Country when they are seeking information in regard to this country, contain so little with regard to the province of Ontario that intending immigrants receive no encouragement from that source to come to that province. This is a matter I have endeavoured to press not only upon this government but upon the previous government on numerous occasions. I may observe that I am referring to the reports in connection with the experimental farms of this country, from which you will find that there is practically no effort being made to do justice to the wonderful possibilities we have in that province.

The history of immigration work in Ontario is just as I have endeavoured to point out. The work was handed over to the federal government in 1902 and for a number of years they controlled it until the provincial government were finally forced to adopt the method to which I have

referred and establish their own agencies in the Old Land again. At that time there was a conflict, because while the federal government were paying a bonus of $5 to the booking agents for every immigrant booked to Canada, no commission was given for any immigrant sent to the Ontario government's agency. This was the case until 1908 or 1909, when the Ontario government again entered upon this work in the Old Land. And if they do not see fit now to give up their office and agencies the reason I think is obvious. Now the minister says he is prepared to print literature for the province.

member has mistaken what I said. I said I would distribute literature for the provinces; and even if the government of Ontario cares to maintain its office, as I am quite willing that it should do, it may use every federal agent we have to advertise the province.

speechtext:
The fact that immigration comes within the scope of the federal government and not of the provincial government would justify the Dominion in giving impartial treatment to all the provinces. I doubt whether there is in the whole' Dominion a place which is so well adapted as Ontario for the bringing in of immigrants, particularly if they lack the experience to start on their own resources. They come into Ontario, however, and after they have obtained some degree of experience the fall excursions for farm labourers are advertised all over the province and these people go to the West and engage in harvesting. Many of them see great opportunities of obtaining cheap lands and they remain out there. I venture to say that tens of thousands of those who have come to Ontario have gone out in that way.
Now, the minister has entered into an arrangement with an organization known as the Canada Colonization Association. I remember seeing this matter featured in the press for a considerable time past, and it struck me as propaganda that was being carried on with an object. When I saw that it was to be purely for philanthropic purposes I became somewhat interested and wondered how it was that such an earnest effort was being .put forth. I followed the proceedings as carefully as I could and noticed that the minister had announcements to make from time to time with regard to government policy. A year ago very little criticism was offered because the government had not been in office very long. But owing to the fact while the war was on there was practically no

Supply-Immigration
immigration to Canada, and that during the past year immigration has fallen off by some 90,000 as compared with the previous year, it was undoubtedly a warning to the government that some effort should be made to meet the situation.
The minister has stated that the Canada Colonization Association has had a rather stormy career lately. In fact from his remarks I rather gathered that he himself was somewhat dubious as to the wisdom of continuing the arrangements entered into with the association. It was characterized by the Prime Minister as a welfare league composed largely of hon. members of a political persuasion opposed to his own, and I was wondering if that was one of the reasons which accounted for his apparent anxiety to favour the association. Certainly to do so would be something unusual. I may say that so far as I am concerned I do not know who are at the head of the Canada Colonization Association, nor am I aware what their political faith is, and I care much less; but I do say that when the government undertake to vote large sums of money to be handed over to land agents with a view to bringing immigrants to this country and placing them under the control of the Soldier Settlement Board, they are leading those people to believe that the government are to some degree at least officially responsible for the treatment which these immigrants are accorded. I shall not go into the history of this association at length because it was dealt with very fully before. When the minister (Mr. Stewart) first brought the matter up I put several questions to him, and it appears now that I was right in the conclusions I had arrived at on that occasion because what I said then has not been since contradicted.
When the Prime Minister pointed out that Sir John Willison had resigned from the presidency of the association owing to the criticisms which were being levelled at it, be asked to have some confirmation from the two groups on this side of the House as to their attitude towards the association. Letters were read by the Prime Minister, and he endeavoured to draw the conclusion that their writers were in favour of such a policy as had been advocated by the government. 1 do not think that conclusion could be reasonably drawn from those letters, for the very fact that the association had received them for that purpose would to my mind bring them under suspicion. If the association are in a position t-o do what they claim, if, as their papers indicate, they have been organized purely on a voluntary basis without any

idea of making a profit then they ought not to resort to these methods.
Let me quote a few articles from the Toronto Globe of September last dealing with this matter. On September 2, 1922, the Globe contained this item copied from a Winnipeg paper:
S. W. Jacobs, M.P., continued his criticisms of the King government's immigration policy and his advocacy of the private ownership of the government railways before the Winnipeg Liberal Association.
On the same date the Globe contained the following despatch from its Ottawa correspondent :
Progress is also being made in formulating an aggressive and prudent immigration policy, and Honourable Charles Stewart, who has had this in charge, has his program about completed, and it was discussed to some extent at to-day's cabinet meeting. It will likely be dealt with again to-morrow by the cabinet, and it is understood that next week the plan for stimulating immigration of the better class of people to this country will be made public.
On the 11th September the Globe had this announcement on its front page, headed "Ministry discloses plan of importing needed citizens."
Careful selection of agriculture workers. Canadian Colonization Association will work in conjunction with British overseas settlement officials, federal and provincial co-operation-
This was evidently the policy which the government decided to adopt on that date. On the following day the Globe contained an editorial headed, "The peopling of Canada , in the course of which the following appeared:
The Canadian people will approve both the aim and method of the federal government's new immigration policy, etc. The services of the Canadian Colonization Association, an organization backed by private capital, which has been a long time mapping out the field for immigration to this country and will have the financial support of the Imperial government, will be employed in the location of settlers.
I should like the minister to inform the committee what financial support this association is receiving from the Imperial government.
